lessons.title: Follow a value through a program

lead.text: A Python program is a list of instructions, written one to a line. Python reads them from the top and carries out each one in turn, so the order you write them in is the order things happen. The most common instruction gives a value a name.

Say a shop sells pens at 4 each. The line price = 4 stores the number 4 under the name price. A labelled jar is a good picture: the name is the label and the value is what's inside. The equals sign here is an instruction to store, and it says nothing about whether two things match. An instruction of this kind is called an assignment.

The right-hand side can be a calculation. For total = price * 3, Python reads price and finds 4, then multiplies it by 3 and puts the answer, 12, in a new jar labelled total. The star is Python's multiplication sign. You can also leave a note for people reading the program: a line that starts with # is a comment, and Python skips it.
Python has reached the line price = 4, and nothing else has run yet. Think about what the line leaves behind once it has finished.

Return to the spreadsheet, where changing A1 rewrote B1 for you. A short program shows how Python differs. Step through the lines in the picture and watch the two names, price and total. The small int label beside each value only says it is a whole number, which the next lesson explains.

afterFigure.text: After line 3, price holds 6 and total still holds 12. When Python ran line 2 it read price, which was 4 at that moment, worked out 4 × 3 and stored the answer. The name total keeps only that answer. It has no record of the calculation behind it, so changing price later cannot reach back and alter it.

The second case in the picture shows the only way to get a total of 18. You run the calculation again, by writing total = price * 3 a second time after price has changed. Python works out each line when it reaches it, and the result stays in its name until a later line stores something else there.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6
total = price * 3

lead.text: Here is the same pattern with new numbers. The program stores price and uses it to work out total. Then it changes price. Decide what total holds at the end.

steps.headline: Changing a name using its own value

lead.text: A line can change a name by building on what it already holds. Take x = 3 followed by x = x + 2. Python always works out the right-hand side first, using the value x holds at that moment, which is 3. It gets 5 and stores that under x, which replaces the old 3.

Storing a new value under a name that already has one is called reassignment. Adding to a name is so common that Python has a shorthand: the line x += 2 means exactly the same as x = x + 2. A running total in a data program is usually built this way, with each line reading the name and putting back an adjusted value.
To say what a name holds at any point, read the lines above that point and apply them in order. Skip the comments, since Python does. Whatever the last line stored under the name is what it holds.
Comments change nothing, so they are easy to trace. Work through the program line by line and ignore anything Python would skip.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
amount = 7
# amount = 100
print(amount)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
amount = 7
amount = 100
print(amount)

lead.text: So far the lines ran from top to bottom in one go. Most data analysis happens in a notebook instead, a page made of separate boxes called cells, each holding a few lines of Python. You run a cell by pressing a button, and you may run any cell, in any order, as many times as you like.

Something has to remember the names between those runs. It is a program called the kernel, which sits behind the notebook and keeps a record of every name and its value. Run a cell that sets count = 2 and the kernel holds count at 2. Run a different cell later and it finds count still there.
Put together, a notebook is one long program that you feed in pieces. The kernel keeps its names until you restart it, and then they are all gone.

steps.headline: A notebook cell sets count = 2. Then a second cell, count += 3, is run twice. What is count?

lead.text: The kernel's memory does the work here. Follow count through each run.

workedSteps.text: The first cell stores 2 under count.
Run the second cell once. count += 3 means count = count + 3.
Run it again. It starts from the value the kernel kept.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
count = 2
count += 3
print(count)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
count = 2
count += 3
count += 3
print(count)

steps.headline: A notebook starts with count = 1. You run count += 4 three times. What is count at the end?

workedSteps.text: Start with count = 1. The first run adds 4.
The second run adds 4 to the kept value. What is count now?
The third run adds 4 again. What is count at the end?

steps.headline: Why the order of runs matters

lead.text: Because the kernel remembers, the order in which you run cells decides what it holds, and that order need not match the order down the page. Say cell 1 sets days = 3 and cell 2 works out hours = days * 24, so hours is 72.

Now go back and edit cell 1 to days = 5, and run only that cell. The kernel holds days at 5, but hours is still 72, because the line that works it out has not run again. Run cell 2 and hours becomes 120. Until you do, the page shows code that no longer matches what the kernel holds.

This is why a notebook can mislead. The page can look right while the kernel holds results from older runs. The check is to restart the kernel and run every cell from the top, in page order. If the results still make sense, nothing in the notebook depends on an old run.
Three cells share one kernel. Think about which value of rate the kernel holds when cell 2 runs for the second time.

blocks.text: Open a spreadsheet and type 5 into A1. In B1 type =A1*4, and B1 shows 20. Now change A1 to 9. B1 changes to 36 without you touching it, because B1 holds a rule and the sheet applies that rule again whenever A1 changes.

Python is a language for giving a computer written instructions, and much of modern data analysis is done in it. It behaves differently from a spreadsheet. When Python works something out it keeps the answer and forgets how it got there. That difference explains most of the surprises a newcomer meets, and it decides which numbers you can trust when you return to a piece of work an hour later.

This lesson follows one number through a tiny shop program. It starts with a single line, to see what Python keeps. After that it moves to the kind of page where analysts usually work, and there the order you run lines in starts to matter.

intro.promise: By the end you'll follow a value through a Python program line by line, and say what a notebook still remembers.

recap.keyIdea: A name holds the value it was given at that line. Python runs lines in order, and a notebook kernel keeps every name between runs.

blocks.text: Back at the spreadsheet, B1 follows a rule and a Python name keeps an answer. You saw total hold 20 after price changed, counted a notebook up to 13 across three runs, and worked out that running cell 2 again reads the newest rate.

recap.nextHook: Every value so far was a number, yet a name can also hold text, and Python treats the text '12' very differently from the number 12. The next lesson sorts out which is which and shares eleven biscuits between four plates.

lessons.title: Know what a number means

lead.text: Start with the file. When a program reads a line such as 11 biscuits, the 11 arrives with quotation marks around it, as text. Python calls every kind of value a type, and it has a separate type for each job. Text is a str, short for string. A whole number is an int, short for integer. The number 12 is an int, and '12' in quotation marks is a str that happens to contain the characters 1 and 2.

The difference matters because one symbol does different jobs for different types. Between two ints, + adds, so 3 + 4 gives 7. Between two strs, + joins them end to end, so '3' + '4' gives '34'. The picture runs both versions with the values '12' and '3'.

afterFigure.text: To get arithmetic out of text, convert it first. int('12') reads the characters and returns the whole number 12, and that happens before + sees the values. Quotation marks make text even when the characters are digits, so a program has to say when it wants a number.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
a = '12'
b = '3'
result = a + b

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
a = '12'
b = '3'
result = int(a) + int(b)

lead.text: Both values below start as text. int() turns each one into a whole number before the + gets to work.

Now the bakery. With both values converted, the program has 11 biscuits and 4 plates. Sharing them out is division, and Python has three division operators because there are three questions you might ask. The answer to a division is called the quotient.

The first operator, /, divides exactly and gives a decimal answer, so 11 / 4 is 2.75. A number with a decimal part is a float. The second, //, is floor division, and it gives the number of whole groups: 11 // 4 is 2, so each plate gets 2 biscuits. The third, %, gives the remainder, the amount left once the whole groups have been taken out. 11 % 4 is 3.

Between them, // and % split a quantity into whole groups and a leftover, which is how the bakery can say two each with three left over. Multiply back to check: 2 × 4 + 3 is 11. One more operator is worth knowing. ** raises a number to a power, so 2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.
The bakery has 11 biscuits and 4 plates. Use what you know about whole groups and leftovers.

So far every number was positive. Negative numbers show what // really does. Floor division rounds down, to the whole number on the left of the exact answer on a number line. For positive numbers that looks like dropping the decimal part: 7 // 2 is 3, because 3.5 rounds down to 3. With a negative answer the two ideas part company. The exact answer to −7 / 2 is −3.5, and the whole number just below −3.5 is −4, so −7 // 2 is −4.
The picture runs the biscuit sum twice. In the first case a is 11 and b is 4, as before. In the second case a is −11.

afterFigure.text: In the second case the exact answer is −2.75, and rounding down gives −3, not −2. The remainder follows from the quotient. It is what is left after the whole groups are taken back out, so −11 − (−3 × 4) = −11 + 12 = 1. When the number you divide by is positive, the remainder is never negative, even if the number being divided is.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
a = 11
b = 4
quotient = a // b
remainder = a % b
exact = a / b

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
a = -11
b = 4
quotient = a // b
remainder = a % b
exact = a / b

workedSteps.text: Divide exactly first.
// rounds down, towards the smaller number, not towards zero.
The remainder is what the whole groups leave behind.
Divide exactly.
Round down. Which whole number sits just below −2.6?
The remainder is −13 minus (that whole number × 5). What is it?

lead.text: Back to / for a moment. Its answers are floats, and floats have a limit you should know about before trusting them with money. A computer stores a float using only 0s and 1s, and in that system some decimals have no exact form, just as one third has no exact decimal form: 0.333 and so on without end. The decimal 0.1 is one of the awkward ones. Python keeps the nearest value it can, which is very slightly off.

Usually the error is far too small to see. It shows when you compare. The symbol == asks whether two values are equal and answers True or False, a value of type bool. The sum 0.1 * 3 comes out as 0.30000000000000004, so 0.1 * 3 == 0.3 is False even though the two sides agree on paper. That is why money is often held in whole pence, and why exact comparisons of floats are avoided.
Whole numbers have no such problem. An int is stored exactly, and it can grow as large as the computer's memory allows.
Work out whether the two sides of the comparison hold exactly the same stored value.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
value = 2 ** 40
exact = value + 1

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
total = 0.1 + 0.2
equal = total == 0.3

lead.text: Comparisons give True or False, and Python can read any other value as a yes or no in the same way. The function bool() shows how it reads a value. Zero gives False. The value False gives False. Empty text, written '' with nothing between the quotation marks, gives False. Every other value gives True.

That rule catches people out with data from files, where everything arrives as text. The string 'False' has characters in it, so bool('False') is True. So is bool('0'). All Python checks is whether any characters are there, and what they spell makes no difference. To test for the word False, compare the text with 'False' or convert it first.
A blank field in a file arrives as empty text, so bool() is a quick way to spot a missing entry.
Four values go through bool(). Decide for each whether Python reads it as yes or no, then count the yeses.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
value = False
flag = bool(value)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
value = 'False'
flag = bool(value)

blocks.text: A bakery keeps its orders in a file, and one line reads 11 biscuits, 4 plates. Someone wants to know how many biscuits each plate gets and how many are left in the box. You can do that in your head: two each, with three left over. Getting Python to say it takes a little more care.

Python needs to know what kind of thing each value is before it will do anything with it. A file hands over everything as text, so the 11 and the 4 arrive looking like numbers without being numbers. Add them as they stand and they stick together instead of giving 15.

This lesson follows those two values from the file to an answer. First comes telling text from numbers and converting one into the other. Next the biscuits are shared out, which takes three kinds of division and raises a question about negative numbers. The last two stops are places where numbers surprise people: decimals that are slightly off, and what Python counts as true.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell text from numbers in Python, and use / and // and % to split a quantity exactly.

recap.keyIdea: A value's type decides what an operator does. Convert text before doing sums, and use // and % to split a quantity into whole groups and a leftover.

blocks.text: Back at the bakery, you shared 11 biscuits as 2 each with 3 left over. Along the way you found that −13 // 5 is −3, that a sum of decimals can miss its target by a hair, and that two of the four values you tested count as True.

recap.nextHook: A piece of text is a row of characters, and the next lesson cuts out exactly the characters you want, using positions that start at zero like the marks on a ruler.

lessons.title: Take exactly the text you need

lead.text: Take the word CRAYON. Python sees six characters in a row, and each one has a number called its index, which says how far along the row it sits. The first character is zero steps along, so C has index 0. R is one step along, so it has index 1. The row ends with N at index 5. Counting from zero feels odd at first, but a ruler does the same, because its first mark is 0.

You ask for a character by writing the word and then its index in square brackets. With word = 'CRAYON', word[2] is 'A'. The function len(word) gives the number of characters, which is 6, so the last index is always one less than the length. You can also count back from the end. A negative index starts at the far side, so word[-1] is the last character, N, and word[-2] is the one before it.

One character at a time is slow when you want a whole piece of a word. For that you give two numbers with a colon between them, as in word[1:4], and the result is called a slice. Picture a ruler laid along the word with its marks falling between the characters: mark 0 sits before the first character, and each further mark sits after the next one. A slice runs from its start mark to its stop mark.

So word[1:4] takes everything between marks 1 and 4, which is the characters at index 1, 2 and 3. The start is included and the stop is left out, and that is why a slice is as long as the stop minus the start. Step through the picture, where label[1:4] takes 'LAN' out of 'PLANET'.

afterFigure.text: Check it against the ruler. The piece between marks 1 and 4 is 4 − 1 = 3 characters long, just as the pencil in the opening was 5 − 2 = 3 cm. The second case in the picture counts from the end. The slice label[-2:] starts two marks from the end and, because the stop is empty, carries on to the end of the word, which gives 'ET'.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
label = 'PLANET'
part = label[1:4]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
label = 'PLANET'
part = label[-2:]

lead.text: A slice takes the characters from its start up to, but leaving out, its stop. Apply that to the word below.

A slice does not need both numbers. If the start is missing, the slice begins at the front of the word, so word[:3] gives the first three characters. A missing stop sends it to the end, so word[3:] gives everything from index 3 onwards. Missing both, word[:] is the whole word.

Negative numbers work in a slice as they do for a single character, by counting back from the end. That makes it easy to take the last few characters of a word without knowing how long it is. The slice word[-5:] starts five back from the end and runs to the end, so it always gives the last five characters, whatever the word. It is the tool for pulling a file extension or a country code off the end of some text.

steps.headline: Take the last four characters of 'HARVEST'.

lead.text: The same two ideas, a negative start and an empty stop, take a piece off the end.

workedSteps.text: A negative start counts back from the end. Four back from the end is -4.
Leaving the stop empty means: carry on to the end of the string.
Positions start at 0. The slice starts at position 1 and stops before position 5.
Count the positions from 1 up to, but not including, 5. How many is that?

lead.text: Slicing takes text apart. Often the job is to tidy it, because data arrives with stray spaces and mixed capitals. Python gives every string a set of built-in actions called methods. You call a method by putting a dot after the string, then the method's name with brackets after it. The method name.strip() removes spaces from both ends of name, and name.upper() turns its letters into capitals.

A method cannot edit the string it was called on, because a string cannot be changed once it exists. It builds a new string and hands it back, and the original stays exactly as it was. To keep the tidy version, store it under a name, as in clean = name.strip().upper().

afterFigure.text: In the picture, the first case stores the cleaned text under clean, and name still holds the padded original. The second case runs the same methods but stores nothing, so the tidy text is made and thrown away at once. Methods can be chained like this: strip runs first, and upper runs on whatever strip handed back.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
name = '  bay  '
clean = name.strip().upper()

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
name = '  bay  '
name.strip().upper()

lead.text: A string method builds a new string. Think about what becomes of that new string when the line does not store it anywhere.

Some characters are invisible, and a line break is one of them. Inside a quoted string you write a line break as a backslash followed by the letter n. Python turns those two keystrokes into a single newline character. This kind of shorthand is called an escape. A string with an escape between two letters holds three characters and prints on two lines.

The code you see does not always match the length Python reports. The function len counts the characters in the finished string, and an escape adds one, no matter how many keystrokes it took. Spaces and tabs add to it too, so stray spaces at the ends of data are worth removing.
Count the characters in the finished string, which may not match the keystrokes you typed.

steps.headline: Past the end of the word

lead.text: Slices are forgiving at the edges. If the stop is larger than the word, the slice quietly ends at the last character, so 'ABCDEF'[3:20] is 'DEF'. If the start lies beyond the end, nothing sits between the marks and the result is an empty string, one with no characters at all. A slice never raises an error for numbers that are too large.

A single index is different. Asking for 'ABCDEF'[20] names a character that does not exist, and Python stops the program with an IndexError. That is why slices are the safer choice for short or messy input: they return whatever is there, even if that is nothing. A field shorter than you expected will not break the program, though it may leave you with an empty piece, so check the length when the piece matters.
Picture the ruler laid along the word, and ask where the two marks of the slice fall.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
code = 'ABCDEF'
tail = code[3:20]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
code = 'AB'
tail = code[3:20]

lessons.orientation: Use zero-based indexing, slice boundaries and string methods.

blocks.text: Hold a ruler against a pencil so that the tip lines up with the 2 cm mark and the other end with the 5 cm mark. The pencil is 3 cm long, and you find that by taking one mark away from the other. The marks do the counting, and the first of them is 0.

Text in a program can be measured the same way. A product code, a surname or a date written out in full is a row of characters, and data arrives full of them, usually with something extra attached: spaces at the ends, capitals where you wanted lower case, a year stuck to the front of an order number. Pulling out exactly the piece you need is a job you will do again and again.

This lesson lays a ruler along a word. You learn to name each character by its position and to cut out a piece by giving two marks, and then to clean text up. The last stop is the end of the ruler, where Python is more forgiving than you might expect.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count positions from zero, cut text with [start:stop], and know which string methods change the original.

recap.keyIdea: Positions count from zero. A slice includes its start and excludes its stop, and a string method hands back a new string rather than changing the old one.

blocks.text: Back at the ruler, a slice measures stop minus start. You counted 3 characters in 'ORCHARD'[2:5] and 4 in 'LANTERN'[1:5], saw that a method's tidy result is lost unless you store it, and found that a slice past the end of 'AB' leaves nothing.

recap.nextHook: Text cannot be changed in place, but a list can, and that has a surprising result when two names lead to one list. The next lesson begins with two keys cut for the same locker.

lessons.title: Change a collection without surprises

lead.text: Think of the locker as a Python list: a row of values kept in order, written in square brackets with commas between the items. [4, 7] is a list of two items. The items are numbered from zero, like the characters in a string, so with books = [4, 7] the expression books[0] is 4 and len(books) is 2. Negative numbers count back from the end, and slices cut out pieces, exactly as they do for text.

Unlike a string, a list can be changed after it is made. The method books.append(9) adds 9 to the end of the same list, and books[0] = 5 replaces the first item. Changing a list like this is called changing it in place, because the list itself is altered and nothing new is made. The locker keeps its place and only its contents change.
A list is the locker, and a name is a key to it. The next screen puts a second key in someone else's hand.

Suppose a = [2, 5] and you then write b = a. It looks as though b gets a list of its own holding 2 and 5, but Python only attaches a second name to the list that already exists. Now there is one list with two names, like two keys to one locker. A second name for the same list is called an alias. Whatever you do through b happens to the list that a leads to, so b.append(8) makes the list [2, 5, 8] for both names.

To get a second locker you have to ask for one. The method a.copy() builds a new list with the same items, and b = a.copy() points b at that new list. Step through the picture, where the first case uses b = a and the second uses b = a.copy().

afterFigure.text: In the first case a ends as [2, 5, 8], though the append was called through b. In the second case a stays [2, 5] and only b grows. The difference lies in the second line: assignment adds a name, while copy adds a list. When a list changes and nobody seems to have changed it, the first thing to check is whether two names share it.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
a = [2, 5]
b = a
b.append(8)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
a = [2, 5]
b = a.copy()
b.append(8)

lead.text: Two names can lead to one list. Think about how many lists exist at the moment append runs.

A method that changes a list in place has a quiet habit: it returns nothing useful. Every method hands something back to the line that called it, and append hands back None, the special value that means 'no value'. The list has already been changed by then. String methods trained you to expect the new thing back, so this is easy to forget.

It becomes a trap when you store the result. The line items = items.append(9) appends 9 to the list and then stores the returned None under the name items. The name now leads to None, and the list, though still in memory, has lost the only name it had. The safe habit is to call append on a line of its own and leave the name alone.

steps.headline: With items = [4, 7], what goes wrong in items = items.append(9)?

lead.text: Follow the line items = items.append(9) one step at a time.

workedSteps.text: append adds 9 to the list itself, in place.
append returns None. The = then stores that returned value under items.
The list still exists, but no name leads to it any more.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
items = [4, 7]
result = items.append(9)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
items = [4, 7]
items = items.append(9)

lead.text: A list may hold other lists. A table of two columns can be written [[1], [2]], an outer list whose items are themselves lists. That is where a copy gets tricky. The method copy builds a new outer list, but it fills it with the very same items. When an item is itself a list, the new outer list holds the same inner list as the old one, and not another one like it.

Picture two lockers, each with a small box inside, where the second locker was filled by moving the same small boxes across. The outer lockers are separate, so adding a box to one does not add it to the other. Put something into one of the small boxes, though, and the other locker's matching box has changed too, because it is the same box.

A copy that goes one level deep is called a shallow copy. With a = [[1], [2]] and b = a.copy(), the lists a and b are different, yet a[0] and b[0] are one list. So b[0].append(3) shows up in a[0] as well.

steps.headline: With a = [[1, 2], [3]], b = a.copy() and b[0].append(9), how many items do a and a[0] hold?

workedSteps.text: b = a.copy() makes a new outer list. b[0] is still the same inner list as a[0].
append changed no outer list, so how many items does a hold?
append did change the shared inner list. How many items does a[0] hold?

lead.text: Sometimes you want a row of values that cannot be rearranged by accident. A tuple is a row like a list, written with round brackets: record = ('Bay', 7). Its items have indexes and slices work on it, but you cannot replace an item or append to it. A line such as record[0] = 'Hill' stops with an error.

A tuple fixes which objects it holds. It does not freeze what those objects are. If an item is a list, the tuple keeps pointing at that same list. That list can still be changed. A tuple protects its own slots and has no power over a list that sits in one of them.
Tuples suit values that belong together and should stay that way, such as a shop's name and its opening hours.
The tuple below holds a name and a list. Think about which of the two a tuple is able to protect.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(3)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
record = ('Bay', [1, 2])
record[1].append(3)

lead.text: Lists share more with strings than their indexes. A list slice uses the same marks and the same rule: the start is included and the stop is left out, so values[1:3] takes the items at index 1 and 2. A slice builds a new list, so changing it later leaves the original alone.

Multiplying a list repeats its items. [3, 6] * 2 is the list [3, 6, 3, 6], which has four items. Adding two lists with + joins them end to end, as it does for text. The picture shows a slice in its first case and a repeated list in its second.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
values = [3, 6, 9, 12]
result = values[1:3]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
values = [3, 6]
result = values * 2

lead.text: A list slice follows the same marks as a string slice. Work out which items it takes before you add them up.

lessons.orientation: Follow list aliases, shallow copies, append and tuple immutability.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A school locker holds two books. You and a friend each carry a key, and both keys open the same locker. On your way past, you use your key to put a third book inside. Later your friend opens the locker with their key and looks in.

You can say what they will find, because there is one locker no matter how many keys exist. Programs have the same shape. A collection of values can have more than one name leading to it, and changing it through one name changes it for all of them. Data code runs into this often, when a collection is passed from one part of a program to another and altered on the way. The surprise then turns up far from the line that caused it.

This lesson follows one collection of values through a short program. It begins with how Python holds a row of values you can change. Then a second name is attached to the row, and we watch what happens. Making a true duplicate comes next, along with the places where duplicates fall short. The lesson finishes with a row that can't be rearranged.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell when two Python names share one list, and when a copy keeps them apart.

recap.keyIdea: Assignment shares a list; copy makes a new outer list but keeps shared inner lists; append changes in place and returns None.

blocks.text: Back at the locker, two keys opened one list and a copy gave you a second. You found that a holds 3 items after b.append, that a keeps 2 after a copy, that a list inside a tuple can still grow to 3 items, and that the slice [2, 5, 8, 11][1:3] adds up to 13.

recap.nextHook: A list finds an item by its position, which is awkward on a café's tally board, where you want the tea line wherever it sits. The next lesson looks things up by name instead.

lessons.title: Choose the right collection

lead.text: The tally board is a dictionary. It holds pairs, each made of a name and the value that goes with it, written between curly braces: board = {'tea': 4, 'coffee': 6}. The name in each pair is called its key, and the value is what the key leads to. Write a key in square brackets to look up its value, so board['tea'] is 4.

A dictionary can be changed, like a list. Assign to a key that is already there and its value is replaced, so board['tea'] = 7 changes the 4 to a 7 and the board still has two lines. Assign to a key that is new and Python adds a pair, so board['cocoa'] = 2 gives the board a third line. Each key appears once, because assigning to a key twice replaces the first value and never makes a second line.
Step through the picture, where a shop's stock is kept in a dictionary.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the key 'pen' already exists, so its value changes from 3 to 7 and the dictionary keeps two pairs. In the second case 'lamp' is new, so the dictionary grows to three. Reading a key that is not there is different. board['milk'] stops the program with a KeyError, because the board has no such line.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}
stock['pen'] = 7

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}
stock['lamp'] = 7

lead.text: Assigning to a key can replace a value or add a pair. Look at the key in the program before you decide which happens.

A lookup like board['milk'] fails when the key is missing, and a data program often cannot tell in advance which keys exist. Python gives you two safe tools. The word in checks for a key without reading it, so 'tea' in board is True and 'milk' in board is False.

The second tool is the method get, which takes a key and a fallback. The call board.get('milk', 0) returns the value if 'milk' is a key, and returns the fallback, 0, if it is not. The program carries on either way. A fallback of 0 suits a tally, since a drink that has never been sold has simply sold none.

There is one trap. The word in looks at the keys and never at the values. Take a dictionary of prices. The test 2 in prices asks whether 2 is a key, which it usually is not. To test the values, ask the dictionary for them with prices.values(), so 2 in prices.values() checks the values.

steps.headline: With prices = {'tea': 2, 'cake': 5}, what do 'tea' in prices, 2 in prices and prices.get('milk', 9) give?

lead.text: Try the safe tools on one small dictionary of prices.

workedSteps.text: in checks the keys. tea is a key.
2 is a value, not a key. To test values you would use prices.values().
milk is not a key. get hands back the fallback you gave it instead of raising an error.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

steps.headline: With stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}, what is stock.get('lamp', 0) + stock.get('pen', 0)?

workedSteps.text: lamp is not a key, so get returns the fallback. What does stock.get('lamp', 0) return?
pen is a key, so get returns its value. What does stock.get('pen', 0) return?
Add the two results.

lead.text: The café also keeps a visitors' book. A regular signs it every visit, but a name needs to appear only once. Python has a collection for that, called a set. A set keeps each member once and ignores repeats, so set(['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay']) holds Bay once and Hill once.

A set is written with curly braces like a dictionary, but it holds bare members with no values. It has no positions either, so there is no first member to ask for. You can ask whether something is a member by using in. You can also add to a set with the method add. Step through the picture to see a set made from a list of visits and then extended.

afterFigure.text: A set tells you whether something is in it and never how often. Adding a member that is already there does nothing. A plain set can be changed with add and remove. A frozenset is a set that cannot be changed once it is made. Neither kind has positions, so neither can be indexed like a list. Counting how many different shops appear in a long list of visits is the classic job for a set.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
visits = ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay']
shops = set(visits)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
shops = {'Bay', 'Hill'}
shops.add('Lake')

lead.text: Decide which of the statements fits what you have just read about sets.
Go through the two additions one at a time, and note the members after each.

Two sets can be compared directly, and Python writes the comparisons as operators. Take a = {1, 2, 4} and b = {2, 3, 4}, with the numbers standing for people who signed two different visitors' books. The operator & keeps the members found in both sets, and that result is called the intersection. Writing a | b keeps the members found in either set. That result is called the union, and a member found in both is counted once. Subtraction, a - b, keeps the members of a that b lacks. Step through the picture to see the first two at work.

afterFigure.text: In the first case a & b is {2, 4}, the two people who signed both books. In the second case a | b is {1, 2, 3, 4}, everybody who signed either. Each answer is itself a set, so you can count it with len or combine it with another set.

lead.text: That gives four ways to keep a group of values, and each answers a different need. A list keeps items in order, finds them by position and allows repeats. A tuple does the same but cannot be rearranged. A dictionary finds a value by its key. A set records which members are present and ignores repeats.

The question to ask is how you will look the data up. The third reading in a sequence is a job for a list. The price of tea is a job for a dictionary. Whether tea is on the menu, or how many different drinks were sold, is a job for a set. A question of the form 'which names appear in both lists?' is exactly what & answers once the names are put into sets.
Two sets, and you want only what they share. Decide which operator fits that question before you count.

lessons.orientation: Use dictionary keys for lookup and sets for distinct membership.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A café keeps a chalkboard tally with one line for each drink: tea 4, coffee 6. When three more teas are sold, nobody rubs out the board and starts again. They find the tea line and change the number beside it. If the café starts selling hot chocolate, a new line goes at the bottom.

The board works because every line is found by its name. Nobody asks for the second line or the third. Python has a collection built the same way, and it is the usual home for counts, prices and options in data work, wherever a value has to be found by what it is called and not by where it sits.

A second kind of collection answers a different question: has this name come up at all? Think of a visitors' book where each person signs once, no matter how many times they call in. This lesson builds the board, learns to look up a line that may not exist, and then turns to the visitors' book and to the question of who appears in two of them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll look values up by key in a dictionary and use a set to keep only distinct items.

recap.keyIdea: A dictionary finds values by unique key, and in tests keys while get supplies a fallback. A set keeps each member once.

blocks.text: Back at the café, tea went from 4 to 7 on one line while a new drink got a line of its own. You found that replacing a value leaves the number of keys at 2. Adding a member a set already holds changes nothing. The sets {1, 3, 5} and {3, 4, 5} share 2 members.

recap.nextHook: So far each line has run once, in order. A car park that charges by the length of a stay needs a program that chooses between lines and repeats some of them, and the next lesson shows how if, for and while decide which lines run.

lessons.title: Control which work happens

lead.text: Start with one car. The car park rewards regulars, and the program keeps a driver's visits this month in a name called units. A driver with 10 or more visits pays a fee of 0. A driver with 5 or more pays £2, and everyone else pays £4. To pick between those, the program asks questions with a yes-or-no answer. In Python such a question is called a condition. The condition units >= 10 is True when units is 10 or more and False otherwise.

Python writes a comparison with two equals signs. A single equals sign stores a value, so units = 5 sets units to 5, while units == 5 asks whether it already is 5. The conditions go into an if chain. Its first line is if units >= 10:, the middle line is elif units >= 5: (short for 'else if'), and the last is else:, which has no condition and takes whatever is left. Each of these, with the indented lines under it, is a branch. Python tests from the top, runs the first branch whose condition is True and skips the rest. Step through two drivers.

afterFigure.text: With units = 3 both tests fail, so else runs and the fee is 4. With units = 12 the first test passes, the fee is 0 and the other tests are never looked at. The order matters whenever ranges overlap. A driver with 12 visits also satisfies units >= 5, so the test for 10 has to come first. Put the narrowest condition at the top, or it never gets its turn.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

lead.text: Two lines in the chain can look alike and do different jobs. Read the line units = 5 the way Python reads it.
Follow the chain from the top for a driver with 7 visits. Stop at the first condition that holds.

That settles one car. At closing time the program has a list of the day's fees and needs their total. A for loop does the repeating. It takes a collection of items and runs its indented lines once for each, giving each item in turn a name, so for fee in fees: runs once with fee set to the first fee and again with the second, until the items run out. Often the items are just a run of numbers, and range makes those. range(1, 6) hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. It includes its start and stops before its stop value, the rule slices follow, so 6 is never given out. A third number sets the step: range(3, 12, 3) gives 3, 6 and 9.

To add things up, the loop needs somewhere to keep the running figure. A name that starts at 0 before the loop and grows inside it is called an accumulator. With total = 0 above the loop and total += item inside it, each pass adds one more item to whatever total already holds. Starting at 0 means the first item is added to nothing, so after the first pass the total is exactly that item. Step through two totals.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the items are 0, 1, 2 and 3, and total finishes at 6. In the second, range(1, 8, 2) gives 1, 3, 5 and 7, and total finishes at 16. When all you need is the total, Python's built-in sum does the whole job in one call: sum(range(1, 5)) gives 10.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
items = list(range(4))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
items = list(range(1, 8, 2))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

lead.text: Before adding anything up, make sure you know which values range hands out.

steps.headline: Find total after total = 0 and for item in range(1, 6): total += item.

lead.text: Work through one complete total, from the first pass to the last.

workedSteps.text: range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The stop, 6, is excluded.
total starts at 0, then grows by each item.
Add them.

steps.headline: Find total after total = 0 and for item in range(3, 12, 3): total += item.

lead.text: This time you fill in two of the lines yourself.

workedSteps.text: range(3, 12, 3) starts at 3 and steps by 3. It stops before 12. How many times does the loop run?
The items are 3, 6 and 9. Add them to total. What is total at the end?

lead.text: A for loop knows how many passes it has, because its items are counted out in advance. Sometimes the program cannot know. The car park keeps letting cars in until it is full, and nobody can say beforehand how many that will take. For that Python has the while loop. It is written as while followed by a condition, and it tests the condition before every pass. If the test gives True, the indented lines run and the test is made again. When it gives False, the loop ends and the program carries on below it.

The lines inside have to change something the condition looks at. Otherwise the test gives the same answer for ever and the loop never finishes. In the picture, count starts at 1 and the loop runs while count < 6. Each pass adds to count and adds 1 to turns, which counts the passes. Step through both cases and compare.

afterFigure.text: With count += 2 the values are 3, 5 and 7, so turns finishes at 3. With count += 3 they are 4 and 7, so turns finishes at 2. In the first case the test still gave True at 5, so one more pass ran and carried count past the limit. The test happens only before a pass, never during one.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 2
    turns += 1

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 3
    turns += 1

lead.text: Test the condition before each pass and write down the value count takes. Stop when a test gives False.

Real fee rules seldom hang on one test. A night rate might apply only to a car that arrived after 18:00 and left before 06:00. Python joins tests with three words. and gives True only when both sides are True. or gives True when at least one side is. not turns True into False and False into True. Each side is worked out first and gives True or False. The word then combines those two answers. With x = 6, the test x > 3 and x < 9 asks whether x lies between 3 and 9, and the answer is True.

The symbols & and | look like and and or. On whole numbers they work on binary digits instead. Binary writes a number using only 1 and 0, in columns worth 4, 2 and 1. The number 6 is one 4 and one 2, so it is 110. The number 3 is one 2 and one 1, so it is 011. The operator & compares the columns and keeps a 1 only where both numbers have one. Here only the middle column has two 1s, which leaves 010, the number 2. Use the words for conditions and keep the symbols for work on bits.
Work out each of the three tests for x = 6 on its own before you count how many are True.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
x = 6
within = x > 3 and x < 9

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
a = 6
b = 3
both_bits = a & b

lead.text: The barrier program can now be written out as it was first described. It sets total = 0 and runs a for loop over the day's stays. Inside the loop an if chain picks the fee for that stay, and total += fee adds it to the day's takings. When the stays run out, total holds the answer. A loop with a chain inside it is the shape of most data work, since data arrives as a long list of rows and the question to ask of each row usually depends on a test.

Each tool answers a different need. An if chain picks one path. A for loop repeats over items you already have. A while loop repeats until a test gives False, and the words and, or and not let one test hold several requirements. The program is complete, but the fee rule now sits in the middle of the sum. A till and a website would need the same rule, and copying it into each invites two different mistakes.

lessons.orientation: Trace branches, ranges, loop updates and Boolean conditions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A car park barrier has no attendant to ask how long you stayed. A small program reads the ticket, works out the fee and lifts the barrier. A stay under an hour costs £2 and a stay under three hours costs £5. Anything longer costs £9. Whoever wrote the program had to say what happens for each kind of stay, and the answer is different every time.

At closing time the same program has a second job. It must add up the fee from every car that came in that day, which means doing one small calculation once per car. Nobody wants to write the sum out three hundred times, so the program needs a way to say 'do this for every car' and another way to say 'keep going until the car park is full'.
This lesson follows the barrier program as it grows. It starts by choosing between fees. After that it learns to repeat work, and it ends by combining several yes-or-no tests into one decision.

intro.promise: By the end you'll trace which fee an if chain picks and how many times a loop repeats.

recap.keyIdea: A chain runs the first true branch, a for loop visits each item once, and a while loop tests its condition before every pass.

blocks.text: You followed the fee chain for a driver with 7 visits and found that it stops at the second branch, a fee of 2. The loop over range(3, 12, 3) ran 3 times and totalled 18. You also saw that 5 & 3 is 1, because the two numbers share only their last binary digit.

recap.nextHook: The fee rule now sits in the middle of the end-of-day program. A till, a report and a website all need the same rule, and a copy in each place is one more thing to forget when the prices change. The next lesson shows how to give a rule a name, so it is written once and called wherever it is needed.

lessons.title: Turn a calculation into a tool

lead.text: Here is the till card as Python: def cost(units): return units * 5. This is a function, a piece of code with a name, written once and run whenever it is needed. The first line starts with def and gives the function its name, cost, then lists in brackets what it needs. Each name in the brackets is a parameter, a label for a value the function will be given. Here there is one, units. The indented line underneath is the body, the work done every time the function runs.

Using the function is called calling it. You write its name with the values in brackets, as in cost(3). The value you pass is the argument, and Python attaches it to the parameter, so inside that call units stands for 3. The word return sends an answer back to the place that made the call. cost(3) hands back 15, and total = cost(3) stores that 15 under the name total. The parameter is the label inside the function, and the argument is the actual value from outside. Calling cost(8) afterwards gives the same rule a new argument and a new answer.

Many people expect a function to show its answer on the screen, and print does that. print writes text for a person to read. return does a different job: it hands a value back to the code that called the function, where it can be stored and used in more arithmetic. A function can print, return or do both. Each has its own effect. Step through the picture, where one function returns twice its input and another only prints it.

afterFigure.text: The first function returns 8, so result holds 8. The second prints 8 on the screen, but nothing is returned, so result holds None. None is Python's value for 'nothing here', and a function that finishes without reaching a return line hands it back. The 8 on the screen was shown to the reader and stored nowhere. If a later line needs the answer, the function has to return it.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

lead.text: The parameter x receives the argument. Follow it through the body to the line that sends the answer back.
Showing a number and giving it back are separate jobs. Decide what the caller receives when only the first is done.

The till card said the rate is 5 unless the card says otherwise. A function can follow the same rule with a default, a value a parameter takes when the call leaves it out. In def cost(units, rate=5): return units * rate, the parameter rate has a default of 5. So cost(3) leaves rate alone and gets 15. A call such as cost(3, 7) fills both parameters: values given by position go to the parameters in order, so rate becomes 7 and the answer is 21.

An argument can also be given by name, which is called a keyword argument. In cost(rate=7, units=3) each value is labelled with the parameter it fills, so the order no longer matters. The name tells Python where each value goes. Names also make a call easier to read when several values look alike. Step through the picture and compare a call that uses the default with one that names both values.

afterFigure.text: The first call uses the default rate of 5 and gives 15. The second replaces the rate with 7 and gives 21. Both run the same function, and only the arguments changed.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

steps.headline: With def pay(hours, wage=10): return hours * wage, what do pay(3) and pay(wage=12, hours=2) give?

lead.text: Check both ways of passing values on one small function.

workedSteps.text: pay(3) gives hours the value 3. No wage is passed, so the default 10 is used.
pay(wage=12, hours=2) names each parameter, so the order does not matter.

steps.headline: With def cost(units, rate=4): return units * rate, what does cost(rate=6, units=5) return?

workedSteps.text: Keywords name the parameters. So units is 5 and rate is 6.
Multiply the two. What does cost return?

lead.text: So far the arguments have been numbers, and a number cannot be changed in place. A list can be, and that raises a new question: what does a function do to a list it is handed? Python does not copy the list into the function. The parameter becomes another name for the same list the caller holds, much as two labels can point at one locker.

That gives two different outcomes. A method such as append changes the list itself, so def add_item(items): items.append(9) changes the caller's list, and the caller sees the 9 afterwards. An assignment such as items = [9] only points the name items at a new list. The caller's list is left as it was, because only a label inside the function moved. Step through both cases.

afterFigure.text: In the first case values goes from [1, 2] to [1, 2, 9] after the call. In the second it stays [1, 2]. When you read any function, ask whether it changes the object it was given or only points its own label somewhere else.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
def add_item(items):
    items.append(9)
values = [1, 2]
add_item(values)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
def add_item(items):
    items = [9]
values = [1, 2]
add_item(values)

lead.text: Find the line that changes the list, then decide how many items the caller's list holds afterwards.

Not every rule has to be written by you. Python ships with a large stock of ready-made functions, grouped into modules, which are files of related code. The word import loads a module. After import math, its functions are reached through the module's name: math.sqrt(81) is 9.0, and math.ceil(4.2) is 5, because ceil rounds up to the next whole number.

Typing a long module name over and over gets tiring, so import allows an alias, a shorter name of your choosing. import math as m makes m.ceil(4.2) the same call as math.ceil(4.2). The alias exists only inside your program. The rest of this course imports NumPy as np in the same way. One limit is worth knowing. import loads a module that is already installed. It cannot fetch a missing package from the internet, so importing something that is not installed stops the program with an error.
Treat the alias as one more name for the same module, and work out what the call returns.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import math
result = math.sqrt(81)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import math as m
result = m.sqrt(81)

lessons.orientation: Define functions, pass arguments, return values and import installed libraries.
lessons.reviewLabel: Turn a calculation into a tool
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A card taped beside the till reads: cost = units × rate, where the rate is 5 pounds a unit unless the card says otherwise. Everyone who serves a customer follows it the same way. They take the number of units, multiply it by the rate and say the total. Nothing on the card has to be remembered, and nobody invents their own version.

The barrier program from the last lesson needed a fee rule too, and so do the shop's stock sheet and its website. Copying the arithmetic into each place works until the rate changes, and then one copy always gets forgotten. The card has the right idea. The rule is written once and given a name, and every place that needs it refers to the name.

Python lets you do exactly that. This lesson turns the till card into a named rule. It looks at what comes back from the rule and what happens when a value is missing. It also covers what a rule can do to the things it is handed. It ends by borrowing rules that other people have already written.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a function call and tell what return gives back that print does not.

recap.keyIdea: A function takes arguments through its parameters and hands a value back with return; print only displays, and import makes a module's names available.

blocks.text: You priced a 3-unit sale at £15 with the default rate, called triple(7) for 21 and found that cost(rate=6, units=5) gives 30. You also saw that a function which only prints hands back None, and that m.ceil(4.2) rounds up to 5.

recap.nextHook: Every rule so far was handed values it could use. Real data is less tidy. A form that asks for an age will sometimes come back with the word 'unknown', and int('unknown') stops a program dead. The next lesson shows how to expect that failure, carry on past it and say how much you skipped.

lessons.title: Handle failure without hiding it

lead.text: Turning text into a number is the step where the form goes wrong. int('18') gives the number 18. int('unknown') cannot work, so Python raises a ValueError. An error raised like this is called an exception, and unless something deals with it the program stops. Python lets you deal with it. The risky line goes under try:, and under except ValueError: you say what to do if that exception occurs. If the conversion works, the except lines are skipped. If it raises a ValueError, Python jumps to them and carries on afterwards.

Name the exception you expect. Writing except ValueError catches the failure you planned for and nothing else. A bare except would catch every mistake, even a misspelt variable name, which hides real bugs behind a quiet fallback. In the picture the fallback is 0. Step through an age of '18' and an age of 'unknown'.

afterFigure.text: With '18' the conversion succeeds and value is 18, so the except lines never run. With 'unknown' the conversion fails, the except lines run and value becomes 0. A fallback of 0 is a choice, and it is not always a good one. An age of 0 would drag an average down, which the next screens come back to.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

lead.text: Decide what Python does with text that has no digits in it.
The except lines run only if the conversion fails. Decide whether it fails for this text.

What happens to the bad entry is your choice, and the choice changes the answer. One option is to substitute a fallback and carry on. That suits a count where a missing value really does mean none, such as a drink nobody sold. Inside a loop over the entries, the try line is total += int(text) and the except line is total += 10. A bad entry adds 10 to total in place of its own value, and the good ones add what they hold. With the entries '4', 'y' and '5', total ends at 19.

For ages the better option is to skip. A made-up age of 0 or 10 is a number nobody gave, and it pulls the average towards itself. Skipping leaves the entry out so that only real answers count. In code the except lines simply leave total alone, and with the same three entries total ends at 9. Either way the program carries on, which is the point of catching the exception. What remains to settle is how a reader can tell that entries were left out.

A total built from skipped data looks just like a total built from complete data, and a reader has no way to tell the difference. The remedy is to count what was left out. A second accumulator, rejected, starts at 0 and goes up by 1 inside the except lines. It counts the entries that failed while total adds up the ones that worked. Step through the picture, where each entry is a piece of text to be added.

afterFigure.text: With '2' and '5' both convert, total is 7 and rejected is 0. With '2', 'bad' and '5' the middle entry fails, total is still 7 and rejected is 1. The same total comes from different data, and only the count shows which case you are in. Reporting a share is clearer still. One rejected entry out of 4 is 25 per cent, which tells a reader how much of the data the total leaves out.

cases.label: Case A
Case B

steps.headline: Add up ['3', 'x', '9', '?'] as integers, skipping any ValueError.

lead.text: Work through four entries with the counter running.

workedSteps.text: '3' converts, so it joins the total.
'x' raises ValueError. The except branch counts it instead of stopping.
'9' converts and '?' fails.

steps.headline: Parse ['4', 'bad', '6', '?'] as integers, skipping ValueError entries.

workedSteps.text: 'bad' and '?' are not integer text. How many entries are rejected?
Only '4' and '6' convert. What is the total?

lead.text: Turn the count of rejected entries into a share of all the entries.

The answers usually live in a file, and reading a file brings its own problem. Opening a file ties up something the operating system hands out, and it has to be given back by closing the file. A program that stops half-way can leave it open. The with statement looks after this. with open('answers.txt') as f: opens the file, runs the indented lines and closes the file when they end, even if one of them fails. The object that does this work is called a context manager.

with looks after the file. It does nothing about what is inside. The lines come back as text, so every line still needs converting, and a blank line is an empty string that int cannot read. Decide how to treat blank lines before converting. The method strip removes spaces and the line break from the ends of a string, so line.strip() == '' picks out a blank line and lets you skip it. The rejected count can tell a reader how many there were.
Separate looking after the file from checking what is inside it.

steps.headline: Which file does a name mean

lead.text: Opening 'answers.txt' needs a path, the address of a file. A path with no folder in it, such as answers.txt or data.csv, is a relative path, and Python resolves it from the working directory, which is the folder the program was launched from. It is not the folder that holds the script. Launch the same script from a different folder and the same name can point at a different file, or at no file at all.

That explains a common puzzle. A script works in one terminal window and reports 'file not found' in another, with nothing changed in the code. Before blaming the file, check where Python started. A full path that begins at the top of the drive always names the same place, wherever the program is launched from.
The script is the same every time. Only the folder it is launched from changes.

lessons.orientation: Catch expected exceptions and manage files with a context manager.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A form asked for age. Three people answered: 24, unknown and 36. Anyone working out the average age reads the three answers and sets the middle one aside without a second thought. The average of 24 and 36 is 30, and everyone agrees that unknown is not an age.

A program has no such instinct. Asked to turn each answer into a number, it reaches the word unknown and cannot read it as digits, so it stops with an error message. The work done so far is lost, and so is every answer after the bad one. A form with ten thousand rows will always have a few entries like that.

This lesson is about what a program should do instead. It looks at expecting a failure on purpose and at choosing what happens when one occurs. Then it covers how to report how much data was left out. The second half moves to the files such answers are stored in: how to read one without leaving it open, and how Python decides which file a name refers to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll catch an expected error on purpose and read a file inside a with block.

recap.keyIdea: Catch the specific error you expect and say what you skipped. A with block closes the file, and relative paths follow the working directory.

blocks.text: You averaged the two valid ages to get 30. You skipped 2 bad entries to reach a total of 10, and found that 3 of 5 entries, 60 per cent, were rejected. Three launch folders gave three different files, because a relative path follows the working directory.

recap.nextHook: The ages are clean now but they sit in a list, and a list is built to hold anything. Data work usually means thousands of values of one kind laid out in a grid, such as seats in a cinema or readings from a sensor. The next lesson introduces the NumPy array, which holds a grid of one kind of value and works on all of it at once.

lessons.title: Give data a shape

lead.text: NumPy is the library that supplies this container, and by convention it is imported as np. Its array is a grid of values that all have the same type. A plan with 2 rows of 3 seats, each marked with a seat number, is np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]). The outer brackets hold the rows, and each inner pair of brackets is one row.

An array knows its own dimensions. Its shape lists the number of rows first and then the number of columns, so this plan has shape (2, 3). The attribute size counts every value, which is rows times columns, so here it is 6. Each entry in the shape belongs to one axis, which is a direction along which the grid extends. The attribute ndim counts the axes. A table has two. A hall with several floors needs three, and np.zeros((3, 2, 5)) builds a block of zeros with 3 floors of 2 rows of 5 seats, so its ndim is 3.
The shape is written as a pair of numbers. Read which position stands for the rows.

A list and an array answer to the same arithmetic in different ways. Multiply a list by 2 and Python repeats it: [2, 4, 6] * 2 is [2, 4, 6, 2, 4, 6], a list twice as long. Multiply an array by 2 and NumPy applies the 2 to every value, so np.array([2, 4, 6]) * 2 is [4, 8, 12], the same length as before. Because an array holds one type of value, NumPy can run the same operation over all of it at once, and no loop is needed. Step through both.

afterFigure.text: That is why arrays suit data work. A price rise, a unit conversion or a rescaling is one line applied to the whole grid. It also means the same operator can mean two things, depending on whether its left side is a list or an array, so check which one you hold before you read a multiplication.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
values = [2, 4, 6]
result = values * 2

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([2, 4, 6])
result = values * 2

lead.text: Multiplying an array scales every value. Work out the scaled values before you add them.

steps.headline: An array has shape (3, 4). How many elements and how many axes does it have?

workedSteps.text: Shape gives rows, then columns: 3 rows of 4 values. How many elements is that?
Each entry of the shape is one axis. How many axes does the array have?

steps.headline: The same seats laid out again

lead.text: The same twelve seats could be laid out as 3 rows of 4, 4 rows of 3 or 2 rows of 6. NumPy does this with reshape, which gives back the values in a new shape. np.arange(10) makes the numbers 0 to 9, and np.arange(10).reshape(2, 5) arranges them as 2 rows of 5. The values are read off in order and fill the new rows from the left, so the first row holds 0 to 4.

One rule governs every reshape: rows times columns must equal the size. Ten values fit 2 by 5, 5 by 2 and 1 by 10. They cannot fit 3 by 5, which needs fifteen, because reshape never invents a value to fill a gap and never drops one to make things fit. If the numbers disagree, NumPy stops with an error.
Compare the number of values with what the new shape would need.

steps.headline: What are the shape and size of np.arange(10).reshape(2, 5)?

lead.text: See how the shape and the size follow from one call.

workedSteps.text: arange(10) holds the ten values 0 to 9. reshape(2, 5) lays them out as rows of five.
size counts every element: rows times columns.

lead.text: Counting the rows or columns yourself gets tedious and is easy to get wrong. Give reshape a -1 for one dimension and NumPy works that dimension out for you. It divides the number of values by the dimensions you did give. For twelve values, reshape(3, -1) means 3 rows and as many columns as are needed, which is 12 ÷ 3 = 4. reshape(-1, 2) means 2 columns and as many rows as are needed, which is 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Only one dimension can be -1, because two unknowns could not be told apart. Step through both.

afterFigure.text: The first result has 3 rows of 4 and the second has 6 rows of 2. Both hold the same twelve numbers in the same order. If the division does not come out even, NumPy stops with an error, since a whole grid cannot be made.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(3, -1)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(-1, 2)

lead.text: The columns are fixed. Divide the number of values by the dimension you gave.

One more property follows from an array holding a single type. Each array has a dtype, its data type, such as int16 for a whole number stored in 16 bits or int64 for one stored in 64 bits. A bit is a single 0 or 1, and 8 bits make a byte. Every value in the array takes the same number of bytes, so int16 takes 2 bytes per value and int64 takes 8. The attribute itemsize reports it.

That makes the memory an array needs easy to work out: the number of values times the bytes per value. An int64 array of 50 values takes 400 bytes. A Python int has no such fixed width and grows as its value grows. The fixed width is part of why NumPy is fast, and it has a cost. Each dtype has a largest value it can hold, and a bigger number no longer fits.
Work out how many bytes one value takes, then scale up to all the values.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int16)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int64)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

lessons.orientation: Build NumPy arrays and track dimensions, shape and element counts.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A cinema has 5 rows with 6 seats in each, and every seat is the same kind. The booking system keeps a plan of the hall. Ask it for the number of seats and it multiplies 5 by 6. Ask it to raise every ticket price by 10 per cent and it makes the same change to each seat without anyone going through them one by one. Ask for the plan rearranged as 3 rows of 10 and it lays out the same seats again, with none gained or lost.

A Python list is a poor fit for that job. It can hold anything, so it keeps a note of what each item is. It has no idea that its items form a hall. Ages were fine in a list, but data work usually means thousands of values of one kind in a grid, and a better container exists for them.

This lesson meets that container. It starts with the plan itself and how to read its dimensions. Then it asks how a whole plan is calculated on at once and how the same seats can be laid out again. It ends with the memory each seat takes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read an array's shape, count its elements, and reshape it without losing or inventing a value.

recap.keyIdea: An array's shape lists rows then columns and its size is their product. reshape rearranges exactly that many values, and array dtypes have a fixed width.

blocks.text: You counted 30 seats in the cinema. You found that np.array([3, 5]) * 2 sums to 16, that an array of shape (3, 4) holds 12 elements across 2 axes, and that 18 values reshaped with a -1 into 3 rows make 6 columns.

recap.nextHook: The hall plan can be laid out any way you like, and a plan is only useful if you can calculate from it. The takings for each row, the figure for each column and a price change for just one row are all questions about the same grid. The next lesson shows how to calculate across the right axis.

lessons.title: Calculate across the right axis

lead.text: Start with the request that touches every cell. The sheet is held by tickets = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]). Adding 2 with tickets + 2 gives [[3, 4, 5], [6, 7, 8]]. The single 2 has no grid of its own, so NumPy stretches it to fit the grid and then adds position by position. This stretching is called broadcasting. Multiplying with tickets * 10 works the same way and gives [[10, 20, 30], [40, 50, 60]].

Two arrays of the same shape combine position by position, with no stretching needed. If prices = np.array([5, 7, 9]) and sold = np.array([2, 1, 3]), then prices * sold is [10, 7, 27], which is 5 × 2, 7 × 1 and 9 × 3. Each product comes from matching positions, so the result has the shape of the inputs. In neither case does the code contain a loop.
Decide whether the single number is added once or reaches every element.
The 2 reaches every element before you add the elements up.

The second request goes the other way. Instead of changing every cell, it asks for one number that summarises many. tickets.sum() adds all six values and gives 21. tickets.mean() adds them and divides by how many there are, giving 3.5. Methods like these are called reductions, because they reduce many values to one.

A single total for the whole sheet is rarely what the manager wants. She wants the total for each day and the total for each showing. Those need the grid divided up in a chosen way, and NumPy has to be told which way. That choice is the next idea.

Each direction through the grid is an axis. Axis 0 runs down, from one row to the next. Axis 1 runs across, from one column to the next. The axis you name is the one that gets combined. sum(axis=0) adds down each column and leaves one total per column. sum(axis=1) adds across each row and leaves one total per row. Step through both on the sheet.

afterFigure.text: On the sheet, axis=0 gives [5, 7, 9]. The middle showing sold 7 tickets over the two days, which answers the manager's first request. axis=1 gives [6, 15], the total for each day. The result always has one axis fewer than the grid, so a grid with two axes becomes a single line. mean takes the axis in the same way, so mean(axis=1) gives the average for each row.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=0)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=1)

lead.text: Decide which axis leaves one total for each column.

steps.headline: What does sum(axis=1) give for np.array([[3, 1], [2, 5]])?

lead.text: Add across each row of a small grid.

workedSteps.text: axis=1 adds across each row. The first row holds 3 and 1.
The second row holds 2 and 5.
One total per row.

steps.headline: For np.array([[2, 4], [6, 8]]), what does sum(axis=0) give?

workedSteps.text: axis=0 adds down each column. The first column holds 2 and 6. What is its total?
The second column holds 4 and 8. What is its total?

steps.headline: A row added to every row

lead.text: Broadcasting also works between a grid and a shorter array. Suppose a different amount has to be added to each showing: 10 more tickets for the first and 20 for the second. A line of two numbers, np.array([10, 20]), can be added to a grid with two columns. NumPy lines the short array up with the last dimension and repeats it down the rows, so every row gets the same two additions. The short array's length has to match the number of columns. Step through the picture, where the same grid also gets a single 10.

afterFigure.text: In the first case each row receives 10 in its first column and 20 in its second, giving [[11, 22], [13, 24]]. In the second case the single 10 reaches every cell. When the lengths cannot be lined up this way, such as an array of three numbers against two columns, NumPy stops with an error.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + np.array([10, 20])

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + 10

lead.text: The short array is repeated for every row. Work out the four results, then add them.

The last request was a copy of the sheet, and it raises a question about slices. Slicing an array with a[:2] gives a view, a window onto the same stored numbers and not a new set. A view takes almost no extra memory, which suits large data. It also has a consequence: changing the view changes the original, because the two share one set of numbers. In the picture, b = a[:2] followed by b[0] = 99 changes a[0] as well.

When you want numbers that can be changed freely, ask for a copy with the copy method. a[:2].copy() makes independent storage, and edits to it leave a alone. A list slice behaves differently, since it always builds a new list, so the habit from lists needs adjusting. Step through both cases.

afterFigure.text: With the view, b[0] = 99 shows up in a as well: a becomes [99, 4, 6]. With the copy, a stays [2, 4, 6] and only b changes. When an array has to stay as it was, copy before editing.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2].copy()
b[0] = 99

lead.text: Decide whether the changed array shares its numbers with a.

lessons.orientation: Apply elementwise operations, broadcasting and reductions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A booking sheet for a small hall has two rows of numbers. Row one reads 1, 2, 3 and row two reads 4, 5, 6, standing for tickets sold at three showings on each of two days. The manager has three requests. She wants the tickets sold at the middle showing over the two days, the total for each day, and a copy of the sheet with every figure raised by two.

On paper each request is easy, and each one asks for a different movement across the grid. The middle showing needs one number from each row. Each day's total needs the numbers within a row. The rise applies to every cell. The arrays from the last lesson can answer all three in a line each, provided the direction of the calculation is clear.

This lesson works through those requests on the small sheet. It begins with changing every value at once and moves on to adding up in a chosen direction. It ends with a warning about what happens when you edit a piece of an array.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict an array calculation, choose which axis to combine along, and know when editing a slice changes the original.

recap.keyIdea: Array arithmetic applies to every element, axis=0 combines down columns and axis=1 across rows, and a basic slice is a view unless you copy it.

blocks.text: You found that the middle showing sold 7 tickets over the two days, by adding down a column. You also found that np.array([1, 3, 5]) + 2 sums to 15, and that editing a copy left the original's first value at 7.

recap.nextHook: Every array in this lesson was typed out by hand. Real data usually has a pattern: readings at regular distances along a path, or random draws that have to be repeatable. The next lesson shows how arange and linspace lay values out between two ends, and how a seeded generator makes random numbers that can be reproduced.

lessons.title: Generate values with clear boundaries

lead.text: Start with the surveyor's first method. She begins at 0 and walks along the path in strides of 3 metres, putting a post in each time she pauses. NumPy has a function for exactly this, called arange, short for “array range”. It takes three numbers. The first says where to start and the second says where to stop. The third is the size of each step.

For her path that is np.arange(0, 12, 3). It gives 0, 3, 6 and 9, and nothing more. The 12 is missing because arange counts up from the start and quits before it reaches the stop value, so the stop is never part of the result. Her path does have a post at 12 metres, and arange has left it off the list.
Step through the two cases below. With one number, as in np.arange(5), that number is the stop. The start is 0 and the step is 1, so the last value is 4.
