afterFigure.text: The second case starts at 2 and steps by 3, so it makes 2, 5, 8 and 11. The next value would be 14, which is beyond the stop at 12, so it ends at 11. The step does not have to be a whole number. np.arange(0, 2, 0.5) makes 0, 0.5, 1 and 1.5, and the 2 stays out. To count the values by hand, step up from the start and stop before you reach the stop value.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(5)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(2, 12, 3)

lead.text: List the values the way arange makes them. Begin at the start and keep adding the step, and stop before you reach the stop value.

The surveyor would like a post at the end of the path as well, and she would rather say how many posts she has than how big each stride is. NumPy's linspace, short for “linear space”, works that way. It takes the first value, the last value and how many values to make. It spreads them evenly, with the first at the start and the last at the end.

np.linspace(0, 12, 5) gives 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12, so this time the end of the path is included. Nobody told linspace the gap between posts. It worked the gap out. Five posts have four gaps between them, one fewer than the number of posts, and the 12 metres are shared among those four gaps: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 metres each.
The figure asks for four posts along the same path, with and without the end. Step through both cases.

afterFigure.text: With four posts there are three gaps, so the first case spaces them 4 metres apart, at 0, 4, 8 and 12. The second case adds endpoint=False, which tells linspace to leave the last point out. The 12 metres are now shared among four gaps, so the posts stand at 0, 3, 6 and 9, which is what arange gave at the start. Left alone, linspace includes its end, while arange never includes its stop.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4, endpoint=False)

steps.headline: What are the spacing and the values of np.linspace(0, 10, 6)?

lead.text: The spacing comes from the number of gaps, so find that first.

workedSteps.text: Six points that include both ends have one fewer gap than points.
The span is shared among the gaps.
Step from the start by that spacing.

steps.headline: For np.linspace(2, 14, 5), what are the spacing and the final value?

workedSteps.text: Five points make four gaps across the span 14 − 2. What is the spacing?
The endpoint is included by default. What is the final value?

lead.text: The surveyor now wants to inspect one post picked at random. She numbers her five posts 1 to 5, and she needs the computer to choose among those numbers without any pattern she could predict.

NumPy does this with a random generator, an object that produces numbers that look unpredictable. You make one with np.random.default_rng(), and by habit it is stored in a name called rng. Asking it for whole numbers uses its integers method, so rng.integers(1, 6, size=3) draws three whole numbers, each somewhere from 1 to 5.

The size says how many numbers to draw, and leaving it out gives a single number. Run the same line again with a fresh generator and you get different numbers, much as a die gives a different face on each roll.

The two limits given to integers follow the rule that arange used. The low limit can come up and the high limit cannot. rng.integers(1, 6) can return 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, and it can never return 6. That is why the surveyor, with posts numbered 1 to 5, had to write 6 as the high limit.

Stopping short of the high limit also makes counting easy. The number of different values on offer is the high limit minus the low limit, so rng.integers(1, 6) has 6 − 1 = 5 choices, one for each post. A call such as rng.integers(10, 13) offers 3 values: 10, 11 and 12. The 13 stays out.
The high limit is the one that is left out. Decide which limits would allow the last number you want to come up.
The high limit is left out, so every value the generator returns lies below it.

There is a snag for the surveyor. If her colleague runs the same code tomorrow, a fresh generator gives different posts and the two of them cannot compare notes. The fix is to hand the generator a starting number, called a seed, when you create it.

np.random.default_rng(21) always begins from the same place, so it hands out the same numbers in the same order every time the code runs. A different seed gives a different sequence that is just as fixed. Step through the two cases, where only the seed changes.

afterFigure.text: Both cases ask for six whole numbers from 1 to 6, and they differ only in the seed. Anyone who creates a generator with seed 21 and makes the same call gets 2, 5, 3, 4, 3 and 5. A seed is how an analysis shares its random choices so that other people can check them. It does not make the sample any fairer. A sample that leaves out part of the picture leaves it out every time the code is rerun.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

lead.text: Two generators are each created with the same seed and asked for four whole numbers from 0 to 9. Compare what they return.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
b = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
b = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

lessons.orientation: Distinguish arange, linspace and reproducible random draws.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A footpath across a park is 12 metres long, and a surveyor wants to take a reading at regular points along it. She puts a post in at the start of the path and another every 3 metres after that. When she reaches the far end she is not sure whether the post at exactly 12 metres belongs on her list.

How she asks decides what NumPy gives back. One way is to say how big each step is and let the numbers run until they reach the end. Another is to say how many posts she needs and let the spacing follow. The two ways treat the last number differently, which is exactly what she is worried about.
Later she wants to inspect a few posts chosen by chance, and she wants a colleague to be able to choose the very same ones tomorrow. NumPy can do that too.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the values arange and linspace make, and say what a random seed does.

recap.keyIdea: arange stops before its stop value and linspace includes its end unless told otherwise. integers leaves out its high limit, and a seed makes a random sequence repeat.

blocks.text: You saw that np.arange(0, 12, 3) leaves the post at 12 metres off the list, while np.linspace(0, 12, 5) keeps it. You counted 4 values in np.arange(3, 15, 3) and found that two generators with the same seed differ in 0 positions.

recap.nextHook: Every array in this lesson was built by a rule or by a generator. Most data you will meet arrives some other way, as a file of rows and columns that people filled in, with names across the top and codes mixed in among the counts. The next lesson reads such a file into pandas and checks what came in.

lessons.title: Meet a real table

lead.text: Start with what is inside the shop's file. It is plain text, with one order on each line and the values on a line separated by commas. The first line is different. It holds the names of the things recorded, such as shop, units and price. Everything after it is data. This layout is called a CSV file, short for “comma-separated values”, and almost every spreadsheet and database can produce one.

Open the file in a text editor and the first line reads shop,units,price. The second line reads Bay,2,5 and the third reads Hill,1,8. Each line after the first is one order, which makes it a row of the table. Each comma marks the edge between two values. All the unit counts together make a column. The first line is the header. It names the columns and is not an order itself.

Lines of text cannot be added up or averaged until a program has split each line into its values. The pandas library does that. It is a Python library for tables, and by habit it is imported as pd. The call pd.read_csv("orders.csv") reads the header line and uses it for the column names, then turns every line below it into a row.

What comes back is a DataFrame, pandas' name for a table with named columns. Each column holds one kind of value and each row is one record, here one order. A file with a header and ten lines of orders gives a DataFrame with ten rows. The header became the column names, so it is not counted as data. By habit the DataFrame is stored in a name called df, and the rest of this lesson does the same.
The header names the columns. Think about which lines of the file turn into rows.

Once a table is in, the first thing to find out is how big it is. A DataFrame reports that through its shape, a pair of numbers with the rows first and the columns second. The shop's table has four orders and three columns, so df.shape is (4, 3).

To pick out one column, put its name in square brackets. df['units'] gives the four unit counts as a Series, which is a single column of values with the row numbers beside it. Putting the name in a list, df[['units']], gives a DataFrame that happens to have one column. The two print in a similar way and have different shapes.
Step through the figure for the four-order table. The first case picks the column by its name alone and the second picks it with a list.

afterFigure.text: The Series has the shape (4,), a single number, because it has only one direction to count along. The one-column DataFrame has the shape (4, 1), which is four rows and one column. The rule to keep is that a single name gives a Series and a list of names gives a DataFrame.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df['units']
shape = df.shape

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df[['units']]
shape = result.shape

steps.headline: A table has 6 rows and the columns shop, units and price. What are the shapes of df, df['units'] and df[['units']]?

lead.text: Apply the rule to a longer table.

workedSteps.text: shape gives rows, then columns.
A single name gives a Series: one axis of 6 values.
A list of names keeps a table with that column only.

steps.headline: A DataFrame has shape (7, 3). How many columns does df have, and how many does df[['units']] have?

workedSteps.text: Shape gives rows first, then columns. How many columns does df have?
A list of one name keeps a table with one column. How many columns does df[['units']] have?

lead.text: A real file can have thousands of rows, and printing them all only buries the part you need. df.head(4) returns the first four rows, which is enough to see what the table holds. With no number it returns five. The result is a preview. It is a separate object, so the table you asked about is untouched, and a table with ten rows still has ten rows after you store first_rows = df.head(4).

Shape and head together make a quick check after every read. Shape says whether the table has the size you expected. Head shows whether each column holds what its name promises. A problem is far cheaper to fix at this point than after an hour of analysis built on top of it.

Now back to the code 0012. When read_csv reads a column it guesses what kind of value is in it. A column made only of digits is taken to hold numbers, and a number is stored without leading zeros, so 0012 becomes 12. Each column has a dtype, short for data type, that says what kind of value it holds. df.dtypes lists them, and a column of whole numbers shows as int64.

A product code is a label and not a quantity. Nobody adds two codes together, and the zeros are part of the label. You can tell read_csv to keep the column as text with dtype={'code': 'str'}. Text keeps every character that was written, so 0012 stays 0012. Check df.dtypes after reading, because it shows at once when a column has been turned into something you did not intend.
A code is a label and not a quantity. Decide how the column should be read.
Text keeps every character that was written, so the length of a code is the number of characters in it.

steps.headline: When the commas are not commas

lead.text: The shop's second branch exports its file differently. The values on each line are separated by semicolons. read_csv splits at commas unless it is told otherwise, and a semicolon file read that way finds no commas to split at. Each whole line stays in one cell, and the table comes out with a single column holding text like Bay;2;5.

The separator is set with the sep argument. pd.read_csv("branch2.csv", sep=";") splits at the semicolons and gives the three columns the file really has. This is one more reason to check shape straight after reading. A table with the right number of rows and only one column is the sign of a wrong separator, and you can see it before any calculation runs on the wrong table.
read_csv splits at commas by default. Think about what the lines of a semicolon file contain.

lessons.orientation: Read CSV data, inspect a DataFrame and preserve meaningful column types.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Every Monday a shop emails a file of last week's orders. Someone opens it in a spreadsheet to have a look, and one product code stands out: the code 0012 now shows as 12. The spreadsheet decided that the cell held a number, and numbers have no use for leading zeros, so it dropped them without a word.

A program that reads the file can make the same slip, so the first job with any new file is to check what actually arrived. The checks are short. Count the rows and columns, and see whether any value changed on the way in, as the code 0012 did.
This lesson follows one weekly file from the moment it is read to the moment you can trust it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a CSV into a DataFrame, read its shape, and keep identifier codes from turning into numbers.

recap.keyIdea: read_csv turns lines into rows under a header, shape gives rows then columns, head previews without changing the table, and codes and separators have to be read as they were written.

blocks.text: You saw 0012 turn into 12 in a spreadsheet cell. You counted 6 rows below a header, kept all 4 characters of a code by reading it as text, and found that a semicolon file read with commas has 1 column.

recap.nextHook: With the table in, the next job is to pick out the row you mean. Every row carries a label, much as a locker has a number on its door, and that label can differ from the place where the row stands. The next lesson tells labels from positions and shows how to pick rows with each.

lessons.title: Find the intended row

lead.text: Return to the lockers. A table has the same arrangement. Each row has a label, which is the value stored for it in the table's index, and each row also has a position, which counts its place in the order from 0. The label travels with the row. The position is only where the row stands at the moment.

By default pandas labels the rows 0, 1, 2 and so on, which makes label and position look like one thing. They come apart as soon as the labels are anything else. A table whose index holds 10, 20 and 30 has the label 10 at position 0, the label 20 at position 1 and the label 30 at position 2. Sorting or filtering moves rows to new positions, and each label goes along with its row.

steps.headline: Asking by label and by position

lead.text: pandas has one tool for each way of asking. loc looks a row up by its label, and iloc looks it up by its position. Both take square brackets, and both can take a row and then a column. The i in iloc stands for integer position, which is a handy way to remember which is which.

Take a table with the index 10, 20 and 30, a units column holding 2, 5 and 8 and a price column holding 4, 6 and 3. df.loc[20, 'units'] goes to the row labelled 20 and reads the units column. df.iloc[1, 0] goes to position 1, the second row, and to column position 0, the first column. Step through both cases to see where they land.

afterFigure.text: Both calls reach the value 5. The first found it by asking for the label 20 and the second by counting to the second row. If the rows were sorted into a different order, the loc call would still find the row labelled 20 and the iloc call would find whatever row had moved into position 1. Use loc when you know the label of the row you mean and iloc when you know where it stands.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[20, 'units']

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[1, 0]

lead.text: iloc ignores the labels and counts places. Decide which row place 0 refers to.
loc asks for a label, not a place in the list. Pair each label with its value before you read.

Both tools also take slices, a range of rows written with a colon. You met slices on lists, where the end position is left out. iloc follows that rule. df.iloc[0:2] gives the rows at positions 0 and 1. Labels are different. They need not be numbers or step up by one, so no label obviously comes just before the one you name. That is why a loc slice includes both labels you write.

For the three-row table, df.loc[10:20] gives the rows labelled 10 and 20, and df.iloc[0:1] gives only the row at position 0. The first slice ends on a row that it names. The second stops before the position it names. Step through both cases.

afterFigure.text: In both cases the end of the slice is the number typed after the colon. loc keeps the row with that label, and iloc leaves out the row at that position. When you count the rows a slice selects, first ask which tool is being used. That tells you whether the last number is in or out.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[10:20]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[0:1]

steps.headline: With labels 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, how many rows do df.loc[10:20] and df.iloc[1:3] select?

lead.text: Count each slice with its own rule.

workedSteps.text: loc slices by label and includes both ends: 10, 15 and 20.
iloc slices by position and stops before the end: positions 1 and 2.

steps.headline: With labels 10, 20, 30 and 40, how many rows do df.loc[20:40] and df.iloc[1:3] select?

workedSteps.text: loc includes both end labels: 20, 30 and 40. How many rows is that?
iloc starts at position 1 and stops before position 3. How many rows is that?

steps.headline: A row and a column together

lead.text: So far each call picked rows. Both tools take a second value that picks columns in the same way. The first value inside the brackets is for rows and the second is for columns. With iloc both are positions counted from 0, so df.iloc[0, 1] means the first row and the second column. With loc both are labels, so df.loc[30, 'price'] means the row labelled 30 and the column called price.

Either value can also be a list, which picks several at once. df.loc[[10, 30], ['price']] takes the rows labelled 10 and 30 and keeps only the price column. The figure shows that call next to an iloc call that reaches the same cells.

afterFigure.text: Both calls return a small table holding the prices 4 and 3. The loc call names the rows 10 and 30 by label. The iloc call counts to positions 0 and 2 and to column position 1, because price is the second column. Because the values were lists, the result stays a table with a row for each one.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[[10, 30], ['price']]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[[0, 2], [1]]

lead.text: The first number is a row position and the second is a column position, both counted from zero.

Labels do one more job, and it matters whenever two sets of values come together. Suppose a table has rows labelled 10 and 20, and you add a column to it from a Series, which carries labels of its own. pandas does not paste the values down in the order they are written. It lines the Series up with the table by label first, so each value lands on the row that has the same label. This matching is called alignment.

The figure shows it. The Series holds 8 and 3, written with the labels 20 and 10. The first case assigns that Series as a column, and the second assigns the plain list [8, 3], which has no labels at all.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the 8 carries the label 20, so it lands on the row labelled 20. The 3 lands on the row labelled 10. The order the Series was written in makes no difference. In the second case the list has no labels, so its values fill the rows in order and the 8 goes to the first row. A Series follows its labels and a list follows its places, which is the same split as between loc and iloc.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill']}, index=[10, 20])
df['units'] = pd.Series([8, 3], index=[20, 10])

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill']}, index=[10, 20])
df['units'] = [8, 3]

lead.text: A DataFrame has rows labelled 1 and 2. You assign pd.Series([50, 60], index=[2, 1]) as a new column.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish loc labels from iloc positions and recognise index alignment.

blocks.text: Three lockers stand in a row in a school corridor. Each has a number painted on its door: 10, 20 and 30. The caretaker, who likes to count from zero, calls the first locker place 0, the next place 1 and the last place 2. A student asks for locker 20, and the caretaker walks to place 1.

The number on the door and the place in the row are two separate facts about the same locker, and either can be used to find it. A pandas table has the same two facts about every row. The number is the label and the place is the position, and pandas gives you a different tool for each. Mixing them up is a common way to read the wrong row without any error message.
This lesson asks for rows by label and by position, takes slices of each, and then sees what happens when two sets of labelled values meet.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a row's label from its position, and pick the right one with loc and iloc.

recap.keyIdea: loc reads by label and iloc by position from zero, a loc slice keeps its end label while an iloc slice stops before its end position, and a Series assigned to a column lines up by label.

blocks.text: You found that the locker at place 1 carries the number 20. You read 7 at label 20, and you found that row 1 receives 60 when the Series carries the label 1.

recap.nextHook: Picking a row by label or by place suits a row you can name in advance. More often you know a rule, such as orders of three units or more. You want every row that follows it. The next lesson selects rows by a condition and then adds and changes columns.

lessons.title: Keep the rows that answer the question

lead.text: Say the owner's rule to the table: units of 3 or more. In pandas it is written df['units'] >= 3. The comparison does not pick anything out yet. It is made against every row separately, and the answer for each row is either True or False. For the four orders, with 2, 1, 3 and 4 units, the answers are False, False, True and True.

That column of True and False values is called a mask. It has one entry for each row of the table, in the same order, so the mask and the table line up. Think of a stencil laid over the table: the holes are the True entries, and only the rows showing through the holes are kept. A value exactly at the limit passes a >= test, which is why the order of 3 units is True.

Laying the stencil over the table is written df[mask]. It keeps the rows where the mask is True and leaves out the rest. Each kept row comes through whole, with its shop, units and price still together, so the data on a row never gets separated from the row itself.
Step through the two cases. Both build a mask first and then use it. The first tests units. The second tests the shop name with ==, which asks whether two values are equal.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the mask reads False, False, True, True, so rows 2 and 3 survive and keep their original row numbers. In the second case the shop is Bay in rows 0 and 2, so those two come through. A single equals sign stores a value and two equals signs ask a question, so a test for equality always uses ==. The mask can be stored under a name, as it is here. It can also be written straight inside the brackets.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
mask = df['units'] >= 3
result = df[mask]

values.name: mask
values.display:
0    False
1    False
2     True
3     True
Name: units, dtype: bool

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
mask = df['shop'] == 'Bay'
result = df[mask]

values.name: mask
values.display:
0     True
1    False
2     True
3    False
Name: shop, dtype: bool

lead.text: The test is made on each value separately. A value equal to the limit passes a >= test.

Often one rule is not enough. The owner may want only Bay's orders of 3 units or more. That needs two masks, one for the shop and one for the units, joined so that a row is kept only when both are True. The joiner for “and” is & and the joiner for “or” is |. Each comparison goes in its own brackets, and the whole expression goes inside df[...]: df[(df['shop'] == 'Bay') & (df['units'] >= 3)].

The word and will not do here. It wants a single yes or no for the whole column, and a column of True and False values has no single answer, so pandas stops with an error. The symbols & and | work on each row separately. They also bind more tightly than a comparison does, which is why every comparison needs its own brackets.
The figure joins the same two masks with & in the first case and with | in the second.

afterFigure.text: With &, only the third order passes, since it is the only one that is both from Bay and of 3 units or more. With |, a row passes when at least one test is True, so both Bay orders come through along with Hill's order of 4 units.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df[(df['shop'] == 'Bay') & (df['units'] >= 3)]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df[(df['shop'] == 'Bay') | (df['units'] >= 3)]

values.name: result
values.display:
shop  units  price
0   Bay      2      5
2   Bay      3      5
3  Hill      4      8

steps.headline: Rows are (Bay, 2), (Hill, 6), (Bay, 8) and (Hill, 1). How many pass shop 'Bay' and units above 5?

lead.text: Apply one test and then the other, on the same rows.

workedSteps.text: Find the Bay rows first: the first and the third.
Join the two tests with & and put each in brackets.
Among the Bay rows, only the third has more than 5 units.

steps.headline: Rows are (Bay, 2), (Bay, 5) and (Hill, 7). How many pass shop 'Bay' and units above 3?

workedSteps.text: First test: shop is Bay. How many rows pass it?
Both tests must hold for the same row. How many rows pass both?

lead.text: A mask asks a yes-or-no question of each row. A new column can hold a number worked out from each row instead. Arithmetic between two columns happens row by row, just as array arithmetic happened position by position. df['units'] * df['price'] multiplies the units of each order by that order's own price. Storing the result under a name the table does not have yet, as in df['revenue'] = df['units'] * df['price'], adds a new column.

An assignment does not have to come from another column. df['fee'] = 4 puts the single value 4 into every row of a new column, repeated to fit the table, so the column's total is 4 times the number of rows. Step through the figure, where the first case adds revenue and the second removes a column.

afterFigure.text: The first case adds a revenue column holding 10, 8, 15 and 32, one figure for each order. The second case uses drop, which returns a copy of the table without the named column and leaves df itself as it was. The revenue for the whole shop is then the sum of the new column.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
df['revenue'] = df['units'] * df['price']

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units  price
0   Bay      2      5
1  Hill      1      8
2   Bay      3      5
3  Hill      4      8

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units  price  revenue
0   Bay      2      5       10
1  Hill      1      8        8
2   Bay      3      5       15
3  Hill      4      8       32

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df.drop(columns=['price'])

values.name: result
values.display:
shop  units
0   Bay      2
1  Hill      1
2   Bay      3
3  Hill      4

lead.text: Multiply each order's units by its own price before you add anything up.

The last job is a price correction. The owner finds that Bay's price should be 6, and the change is wanted in the Bay rows only. loc, which you used with labels in the last lesson, accepts a mask for the rows. df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Bay', 'price'] reads the prices of the Bay rows. Adding .sum() would total them. Put an equals sign after it and it writes to those cells instead: df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Bay', 'price'] = 6.

It is tempting to do the job in two steps, selecting the Bay rows first and assigning afterwards, as in df[df['shop'] == 'Bay']['price'] = 6. That is chained indexing. The first step hands back a separate table, and the assignment goes to that table, so df does not change. Older versions of pandas sometimes let it through, which is why it still turns up in old code. A single loc call names the rows and the column together and writes straight to df.
Step through the figure. The first case corrects the Bay prices and the second the Hill prices.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the two Bay rows now hold 6 and the Hill rows keep 8. In the second case only the Hill rows change, to 9. The mask picks the rows, the second value picks the column, and the number after the equals sign is written into those cells only. Rows the mask leaves out are never touched.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Bay', 'price'] = 6

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units  price
0   Bay      2      5
1  Hill      1      8
2   Bay      3      5
3  Hill      4      8

values.name: df

shop  units  price
0   Bay      2      6
1  Hill      1      8
2   Bay      3      6
3  Hill      4      8

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]

df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Hill', 'price'] = 9

1  Hill      1      8
2   Bay      3      5
3  Hill      4      8

lead.text: Only one of these names the rows and the column together and writes to df. Check each line for that.
A table has shops Bay, Hill, Bay and Hill, with prices 3, 7, 3 and 7. You run df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Bay', 'price'] = 10.

lessons.orientation: Build Boolean masks, derive columns and make explicit assignments.
lessons.reviewLabel: Keep the rows that answer the question

blocks.text: A small online shop has four orders on its list. Bay ordered 2 units, Hill ordered 1, Bay ordered 3 and Hill ordered 4. The shop ships an order free when it holds 3 units or more, and the owner wants to see which orders qualify.

On four rows she can check by eye. On four thousand she needs the table to do it, and she needs to state the rule once and have it applied to every row. The same table then has to answer follow-up jobs, such as the takings from each order, or a price entered wrongly for one shop that must be corrected in that shop's rows alone.
This lesson works through those jobs on the four orders. It begins with testing each row against a rule and ends with changing a column in exactly the rows that pass.

intro.promise: By the end you'll filter a table with a mask, combine two conditions, and add or change a column on exactly the rows you mean.

recap.keyIdea: A comparison gives a mask with a True or False for each row, & and | join masks when each comparison is in brackets, column arithmetic works row by row, and one loc call changes exactly the rows you chose.

blocks.text: You found that only one row passes both a shop test and a units test when they are joined with &. You worked out revenue of 33 from three orders, and the price column totals 34 after the Bay correction.

recap.nextHook: Every table so far had a value in every cell. Real tables have gaps: a customer skips a question, or a sensor loses a reading. The next lesson shows how pandas marks a gap, and what a total or an average does when it meets one.

lessons.title: Keep unknown separate from zero

steps.headline: A blank is not a zero

lead.text: Look again at the four survey answers: 2, 0, no answer and 4. The 0 and the empty box mean different things. A zero is an answer. Someone was asked, thought about it and reported that they have no pets. The empty box means that we do not know. That person might have no pets or ten pets, and might equally have skipped the question.

pandas keeps the two apart. It marks an unknown entry with a special value that prints as NaN (short for “not a number”) or as <NA> in some column types. This is a missing value. It is not a number and it is not text, and it does not equal zero or anything else. Whenever a calculation meets one, pandas has to decide how to treat it, and the rest of this lesson is about those decisions.

A column of a thousand answers cannot be checked by eye, so you ask pandas to do it. s.isna() returns a mask, a True or False for each entry, with True wherever the entry is missing. You met masks in the last lesson. This one answers the question “is this entry missing?” instead of comparing with a number. A zero is never flagged, because it is a known value.

Two more tools give the counts. s.count() counts only the entries that are known, and s.size counts every position, known or not. The difference between them is the number of gaps. A mask can also be added up, with each True counting as 1, so s.isna().sum() gives the number of gaps directly. Counting the gaps in each column is a good early check on any new table.
isna() marks only the unknown entries. Think about whether a zero is one of them, then count.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([0, None, 8], dtype='Float64')
missing = s.isna()

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([None, 4, None], dtype='Float64')
count = s.isna().sum()

lead.text: Now the survey needs an average. pandas does not wait for you to deal with the gaps first. s.mean() adds up the known entries and divides by the number of known entries, so a gap leaves out both its value and its place in the count. For the answers 7, a gap and 11, the mean is (7 + 11) ÷ 2 = 9, and s.count() is 2.

That default is sensible, since a gap says nothing about the size of the average. It does mean that the average rests on fewer answers than the table has rows, and count() tells you how many. A mean over 3 known answers out of 300 rows would be a poor summary no matter how tidy its decimals look, so it is worth reporting the count beside it.

steps.headline: What are count() and mean() of a Series holding 6, missing, 10 and missing?

lead.text: The mean divides by the number of known values, so count them first.

workedSteps.text: count() counts the known values only.
mean() skips the missing entries, so it divides by the number of known values.

steps.headline: What is the default mean of a Series holding 4, missing and 10?

workedSteps.text: How many of the three entries are known?
Add the known values and divide by that count. What is the mean?

lead.text: There is another way to deal with a gap, which is to replace it. s.fillna(0) returns the series with every missing entry replaced by 0. That is a decision about the data. It says the unknown should count as a real zero, which is only true if a blank genuinely means none. In the survey it does not, because the empty box was not a report of no pets.
After the fill, the zeros are ordinary known values, so they join the count and pull the mean down. Step through the figure, where the same three entries, 2, a gap and 8, are averaged twice.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the gap is skipped and the mean is (2 + 8) ÷ 2 = 5. In the second the gap is filled with 0 first, so the mean is (2 + 0 + 8) ÷ 3, which is about 3.3. Neither answer recovers what the person would have said. Skipping the gap keeps the average honest about what is known, and filling it adds a value nobody observed. Choose a fill on purpose and say which one you chose.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, None, 8], dtype='Float64')
known = s.count()
mean = s.mean()

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, None, 8], dtype='Float64')
filled = s.fillna(0)
mean = filled.mean()

lead.text: A fill is a choice about the data, and it does not bring the real value back. Decide what a zero fill claims.

The other option is to remove the gaps. df.dropna() drops every row that has a missing value anywhere. When only one column matters, dropna(subset=['units']) looks at that column alone and drops a row only if that column is missing. The rows that remain are all known in that column, and a mean taken afterwards uses only them. Zeros stay, because a zero was observed.

Dropping a row also throws away whatever else the row knew, so it is a choice with a price. The figure shows a table of three shops where Hill's units are missing. The first case drops that row, and the second keeps every row and adds a column that flags the gap.

afterFigure.text: After the drop, Bay and Lake remain with 2 and 8 units. Hill is gone from the table. In the second case nothing is lost. The new column unknown_units holds True for Hill, so later steps can tell known rows from unknown ones. Dropping and flagging are both honest ways to handle a gap, as long as you know which one you chose.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Lake'], 'units': [2, None, 8]})
result = df.dropna(subset=['units'])

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Lake'], 'units': [2, None, 8]})
df['unknown_units'] = df['units'].isna()

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units
0   Bay    2.0
1  Hill    NaN
2  Lake    8.0

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units  unknown_units
0   Bay    2.0          False
1  Hill    NaN           True
2  Lake    8.0          False

lead.text: dropna removes the missing entries, so a mean taken afterwards uses only the known values.

One trap remains, and it catches people who know everything above. fillna and dropna do not change the table they are called on. They return a new cleaned Series or DataFrame and leave the original as it was. If you write cleaned = df['units'].fillna(0) and carry on using df, you are still working with the original gaps.

To keep the cleaning, store the result where you will use it. Assigning it back, as in df['units'] = df['units'].fillna(0), replaces the column. Assigning it to a new name keeps both versions, which helps when you want to compare them. After any clean-up, counting the gaps again with isna().sum() shows whether the job was kept.
fillna returns a cleaned copy. Think about what happens to df when nothing stores that copy.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [1, None, 5]})
df['units'] = df['units'].fillna(0)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [1, None, 5]})
cleaned = df['units'].fillna(0)

lessons.orientation: Detect missing values and understand how cleaning choices affect summaries.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A survey asks four people how many pets they have. Three of them give a number: 2, 0 and 4. The fourth leaves the box empty. When the answers go into a table, the empty box goes in too, as a gap, and whoever works with the table has to decide what to do about it.

A gap is easy to mishandle. Treated as a zero, it says the fourth person has no pets, which nobody told us. Skipped over, it quietly changes an average. What pandas does with a gap, and what you can do about it, decides whether the numbers you report mean what you think they do.
This lesson follows that one blank through counting, averaging, filling and dropping, and ends by checking that a clean-up was actually kept.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a missing value from a zero, and say how a cleaning choice changes a count or a mean.

recap.keyIdea: Missing means unknown and zero means measured nothing; summaries skip the unknowns, and filling or dropping is a choice that changes the result and has to be stored to last.

blocks.text: You kept the zero in the pet survey apart from the empty box. You found that the mean of 4, a gap and 10 is 7, and that a column cleaned without storing the result still has 1 missing value.

recap.nextHook: Gaps are the problems a table admits to. Other problems look like data and are not tidy: names with stray spaces, capital letters in some entries and not in others, two facts squeezed into one cell. The next lesson cleans text columns so that matching and counting work.

lessons.title: Turn messy text into usable columns

lead.text: Put the tally sheet into a pandas Series with one entry per tally: 'Bay', ' bay', 'BAY ' and 'Hill'. Ask pandas how many different shops there are and it answers four. It compares text character by character, so a space counts as a character like any other, and a capital B is a different character from a small b. You read past those differences without noticing, but the computer has no way to.

So the text has to be made consistent before anything is counted or matched. Two small jobs cover most of it. Stripping removes blank characters from both ends of an entry, which turns ' bay' into 'bay'. Lowercasing turns every capital into its small form, which turns 'BAY' into 'bay'. Once both have been done, the three spellings of Bay are one piece of text and Hill is unchanged.

A real sheet has thousands of entries, and writing a loop to tidy each one would be slow to write and slow to read. pandas has a shortcut for applying a text job to a whole column, which is where we go next.

steps.headline: One call for the whole column

lead.text: Put .str in front of a method and pandas applies that method to every entry in the Series. s.str.strip() strips each entry and s.str.lower() lowercases each one. The .str part is called an accessor. It is a doorway on the Series that opens onto the text methods, so you can skip the loop and ask for the job once.

The figure runs this on three entries that need tidying: ' Bay ', 'HILL' and ' lake'. The first case only strips them. The second chains another call on the end, so each entry is stripped and then lowercased.

afterFigure.text: Chaining works because every .str call returns a new Series, ready for the next call. It also means the original is untouched, so store the result if you want to keep it, for example clean = s.str.strip().str.lower(). Apply that to the tally sheet and the three spellings of Bay become one entry, which leaves two different shops in the column.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([' Bay ', 'HILL', ' lake'])
result = s.str.strip()

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([' Bay ', 'HILL', ' lake'])
result = s.str.strip().str.lower()

lead.text: strip removes blank characters at the ends, and lower changes capitals to small letters. Neither adds or removes a letter.

reveal.text: You cleaned the text before counting. Case conversion changes letters but keeps their number, so only the spaces were lost.

lead.text: Cleaning makes entries consistent, but a cell can still hold two facts. Suppose the supplier's export writes each row as 'Bay|east', the shop and its region joined by a bar. To count shops by region you need those two parts in separate columns.

s.str.split('|', expand=True) cuts every entry at the bar and gives each piece its own column. Without expand=True you would get a list of pieces inside each cell, which is awkward to use. The figure splits two small Series and names the new columns afterwards.

afterFigure.text: Both cases pass n=1, which tells split to stop after the first bar. In the first case every entry has one bar, so n=1 changes nothing. In the second case 'Bay|east|harbour' has two bars. The shop is 'Bay' and the rest, 'east|harbour', stays together in the second column. That matters when a later piece may contain the separator itself and should not be torn apart.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['Bay|east', 'Hill|west'])
parts = s.str.split('|', n=1, expand=True)
parts.columns = ['shop', 'region']

values.name: parts
values.display:
shop region
0   Bay   east
1  Hill   west

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['Bay|east|harbour', 'Hill|west'])
parts = s.str.split('|', n=1, expand=True)
parts.columns = ['shop', 'description']

values.name: parts
values.display:
shop   description
0   Bay  east|harbour
1  Hill          west

steps.headline: Split ['Bay|east|harbour', 'Hill|west|dock'] once at '|' with expand=True. What does the second column hold?

workedSteps.text: n=1 splits at the first '|' only. The first column is the shop.
The second column keeps everything after that first '|'.

steps.headline: Splitting each of two strings once with expand=True gives a small table. How many cells does it hold?

workedSteps.text: Each string splits into two fields. How many columns does the result have?
There is one row per string. How many cells is that in total?

steps.headline: A rule of your own for every value

lead.text: The .str methods cover cleaning and splitting, but sometimes you need a rule they do not offer. Say each entry lists colours, as in 'red,blue', and you want the number of colours in each. Series.map takes a function and calls it once on every value, then collects the answers into a new Series. A lambda is a small function written on one line, and lambda text: len(text.split(',')) splits an entry at its commas and counts the pieces.
The figure has two versions of the same job.

afterFigure.text: The first case uses map, so the function is called once per entry. The second needs no function at all. s.str.count(',') + 1 counts the commas in each entry and adds one, because an entry with one comma holds two items. That is a vectorised operation: a single instruction that works on the whole column at once. Prefer it when it can express your rule, since it is shorter, easier to read and much faster on a long column. Keep map for rules that no built-in operation covers.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['red,blue', 'green'])
counts = s.map(lambda text: len(text.split(',')))

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['red,blue', 'green'])
counts = s.str.count(',') + 1

lead.text: Series.map is a method of one Series, and it calls the function once for each value in that Series. Decide what the function receives each time.
s.str.count(',') counts the commas in each value. One more than that is the number of items in a comma-separated list.

reveal.text: Counting separators gave the items per value in one vectorised step. You then added the counts to get the total.

steps.headline: Rules that need a whole row

lead.text: Some rules need more than one value at a time. To add the a column to the b column for each order, the function has to see both numbers from the same row. df.apply(f, axis=1) calls f once for each row, and inside f the expression row['a'] reads that row's value in column a. The axis=1 asks for one row at a time. The default, axis=0, would hand over whole columns instead.
The figure adds two columns both ways.

afterFigure.text: The first case uses apply with a lambda. The second does the same sum as df['a'] + df['b'] and then renames the new column with df.rename. Both give the same numbers. Use apply when the rule needs steps that column arithmetic cannot express, such as choosing between two formulas by the values in the row. When plain arithmetic on the columns will do, that is the form to write. The tally sheet is now tidy and split where it needed splitting, and any rule you add can be run row by row or on the whole column.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [2, 4], 'b': [3, 6]})
df['total'] = df.apply(lambda row: row['a'] + row['b'], axis=1)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [2, 4], 'b': [3, 6]})
df['total'] = df['a'] + df['b']
df = df.rename(columns={'total': 'combined'})

lead.text: With axis=1, apply hands the function one row at a time. Inside it, row['a'] is that row's value in column a. Adding up the results is a separate step.

reveal.text: The function ran once for each row and combined that row's two values. The vectorised version does the same arithmetic without calling a function.

lessons.orientation: Clean and split strings, rename columns and choose vectorised or rowwise work.
lessons.reviewLabel: Turn messy text into usable columns
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Picture a tally sheet from a market stall, filled in by three people over a week. One writes Bay. Another writes ' bay' with a space slipped in front, and a third writes 'BAY ' in capitals with a space at the end. Hill is written down once, tidily. A person reads that as two shops. A computer that compares text exactly sees four different pieces of text.

The last lesson was about gaps, which a table admits to by showing them as NaN. These slips are harder because they look like ordinary data, so nothing warns you and a count or a match goes quietly wrong. Some cells hold two facts squeezed into one, such as a shop and its region joined by a bar.
This lesson cleans the sheet until each shop is written one way. It then splits the cells that hold two facts, and ends with how to apply a rule of your own to every row.

intro.promise: By the end you'll clean and split text in a column, and know when a one-line operation replaces a loop.

recap.keyIdea: The .str accessor cleans and splits text for every row at once, and a vectorised operation does what a rowwise function would, in one step.

blocks.text: You cleaned the tally sheet until Bay appeared once, which left 2 different shops. Splitting two strings once made 4 cells, and a rowwise product over the rows (2, 3) and (4, 1) summed to 10.

recap.nextHook: Clean text is still only text. A date such as 03/04/2026 is text too, and it can be read two ways depending on who wrote it. The next lesson turns date strings into real dates by stating their format, and counts the entries that cannot be read at all.

lessons.title: Read a date without guessing

lead.text: pandas can turn a column of date text into real dates with pd.to_datetime. To do it correctly it needs to know which field is which. For 03/04/2026 there are two sensible answers, and you tell pandas which one you mean with a format. A format is a short pattern that names each field in order: %d is the day, %m is the month and %Y is the four-digit year, with the slashes copied as they appear in the text.
So format='%d/%m/%Y' reads 03/04/2026 as day 3 of month 4, which is 3 April. format='%m/%d/%Y' reads the same text as month 3, day 4, which is 4 March. The figure runs both on the invoice date.

afterFigure.text: Neither answer is wrong, since each matches a real convention. The mistake is leaving pandas to guess. A guess can be right for one file and wrong for the next, and the dates it gets wrong look perfectly valid, so nothing warns you. Stating the format makes the reading a written decision that anyone can check, and an entry that does not fit the format raises an error instead of being quietly misread.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['03/04/2026'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%d/%m/%Y')

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['03/04/2026'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%m/%d/%Y')

lead.text: The format lists the fields in the order they appear in the text. Match the text to the format one field at a time.

reveal.text: You followed the format, not a regional habit. %d came first, so the first field was the day and the middle field the month.

lead.text: A format fixes the layout, but it cannot make every entry a date. Real columns hold typing slips, placeholders and impossible dates. '2026-02-30' fits the pattern year-month-day and still does not exist, because February 2026 ends on the 28th. And 'bad' fits nothing at all.

By default to_datetime stops with an error at the first entry it cannot read. That is safe, but awkward for a column of thousands. Passing errors='coerce' tells it to carry on and put NaT in place of each entry it cannot read. NaT, short for not a time, is the missing value for dates, the counterpart of NaN for numbers. The figure parses two small Series that way.

afterFigure.text: Both entries in the first case are real dates, so both parse. In the second case '2026-02-30' does not exist. It becomes NaT, and isna().sum() on the result reports one failure. Make that count a habit, because a coerced column no longer shows what failed, only that something is missing. The count is your evidence of how much of the column could not be read.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['2026-02-28', '2026-03-01'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%Y-%m-%d', errors='coerce')

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['2026-02-30', '2026-03-01'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%Y-%m-%d', errors='coerce')
invalid = dates.isna().sum()

steps.headline: With format='%Y-%m-%d' and errors='coerce', how many of '2026-06-31', '2026-07-01' and '2026-07-02' fail to parse?

workedSteps.text: Check each date against the calendar. June has 30 days, so June 31 does not exist.
The coerced result for the invalid date is a missing date.
The other two are real dates. Count the failures.

steps.headline: With format='%Y-%m-%d' and errors='coerce', how many of '2026-02-30', '2026-03-01' and 'bad' fail?

workedSteps.text: February 2026 has 28 days. How many of the first two entries are real dates?
'bad' is not a date at all. How many of the three entries fail to parse?

lead.text: Dates do not always arrive as text. Systems often store a moment as a single number that says how much time has passed since a fixed starting point. The most common starting point is the Unix epoch, midnight at the start of 1 January 1970 in UTC, and an epoch number counts the time elapsed since then.

The number alone does not say what it counts. A 60 might be sixty seconds or sixty milliseconds, and those moments are far apart. pandas cannot tell, so you say so with unit='s' for seconds or unit='ms' for milliseconds. Adding utc=True marks the results as UTC times so that no local time zone creeps in. The figure converts the numbers 0 and 60 both ways.

afterFigure.text: In the first case 0 becomes the epoch itself and 60 becomes one minute later. In the second case the same 60 counts milliseconds, so it lands a fraction of a second after the epoch. The numbers are identical and the dates differ, which is why you ask whoever produced the data for the unit before you convert. A wrong unit gives dates that look plausible and are wrong.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([0, 60]), unit='s', utc=True)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([0, 60]), unit='ms', utc=True)

lead.text: A bare number carries no scale of its own, so pandas has to be told what one step of it means.
With unit='s', each step of an epoch number is one second. A minute holds 60 seconds.

reveal.text: Both offsets counted seconds, so their difference was seconds too. You then divided by 60 to get minutes.

lead.text: Real dates can be subtracted, and the result is a duration, a length of time whose .days part is the number of whole days in it. The calendar looks after the length of each month, so you never count them yourself.

A column of dates also has a .dt accessor, which works like .str but reads calendar fields such as the year, the month or the day of the week. dates.dt.month gives the month number of every entry, with 1 for January. The figure shows the months of two dates, and then the days between two dates in April.

afterFigure.text: The first case reads the months of 2 April and 3 May, which are 4 and 5. The second subtracts 2 April from 5 April and reads .days, which gives 3. When two dates fall in different months the subtraction still works, because it counts days on the calendar and does not compare day numbers.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(['2026-04-02', '2026-05-03']))
months = dates.dt.month

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(['2026-04-02', '2026-04-05']))
days = (dates.iloc[1] - dates.iloc[0]).days

lead.text: Subtracting two dates gives a duration, and .days reads its whole days. February 2026 has 28 days.

reveal.text: The calendar counted the days left in February and then added the days into March. Subtracting dates handles month lengths for you.

lessons.orientation: Parse known date formats, retain invalid-date evidence and state epoch units.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Two suppliers send you an invoice on the same day. One is in Manchester and the other in Chicago, and both are dated 03/04/2026. The Manchester clerk wrote the day first, so it means 3 April. The Chicago clerk wrote the month first, so it means 4 March. The digits are identical, and nothing in them says which habit produced them.

The last lesson made text consistent. A date is a stricter kind of text, because once pandas has read it as a real date you can sort by it, subtract one from another and group by month. Reading it correctly is the hard part. A column may also hold entries that look like dates and are impossible, such as 30 February, and times sometimes arrive as plain numbers counting from a starting moment, with no hint of the unit.
This lesson follows invoice dates through those problems and ends by working out how many days lie between two of them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read dates with a stated format and count the failures. You'll also convert time given as a plain number.

recap.keyIdea: State the date format, count the dates that fail to parse, and say the unit of an epoch number before you convert it.

blocks.text: You read 03/04/2026 as month 4 under the day-first rule. You found 2 failures among three entries, and 4 days between 26 February and 2 March.

recap.nextHook: Dates are now real dates and the text around them is clean. A table in that state can be summarised, and the first choice is which single figure should stand for many values. When a few values sit far above the rest, the average and the middle tell different stories. The next lesson chooses between them and then works them out inside groups.

lessons.title: Summarise the right observations

lead.text: Go back to the firm. Sharing the wage bill equally gives the mean, which is the sum of the values divided by how many there are. The four wages total 28 thousand, so the mean is 28 ÷ 4 = 7 thousand. It uses how big every value is, which lets one very large wage pull it upwards until it sits above three of the four people.

The median asks a different question. Sort the values and take the one in the middle. With an even number of values there are two in the middle, 3 and 4 here, so the median is their average, 3.5. The 19 could be 190 and the median would not move, since it only cares where each value sits in the order. The figure computes both for the firm and then asks describe() for a fuller summary.

afterFigure.text: The first case prints the mean, 7.0, and the median, 3.5. The second, describe(), lists the count, the mean, the spread and the smallest and largest values, with the 25%, 50% and 75% points of the sorted values between them. The 50% row is the median. Neither figure is right in general. The mean suits a question about totals, such as what each person would get from an equal split. The median suits a question about a typical person when a few values are extreme.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, 3, 4, 19])
mean = s.mean()
median = s.median()

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, 3, 4, 19])
summary = s.describe()

lead.text: The mean shares the total equally, so it uses every value, including a large one. Add the values first, then divide by how many there are.

reveal.text: You shared the total equally, and one large value pulled the result above the others. That is why the median is also reported.

lead.text: A very large value changes how big the total is, but it only changes one position in the sorted order. Decide which summary follows how big the values are.

A single figure for a whole table can hide its shape. Take orders from two shops, where Bay and Hill each appear on two rows with their own units. The owner wants a total for each shop and not one grand total. Grouping does that. df.groupby('shop') puts the rows with the same shop together, and ['units'].sum() then adds the units inside each group.

The result has one row for each shop, because every group is boiled down to a single answer. Any summary can take the place of sum, and mean, median and count work the same way. The figure groups four orders by shop and summarises the units twice, once with sum and once with mean. The as_index=False in the call keeps the shop names as an ordinary column.

afterFigure.text: Bay's two orders are 2 and 3 units and Hill's are 1 and 4. The sum is 5 for each shop and the mean is 2.5 for each. The shops come out equal only because these four rows were chosen that way. What matters is that each answer was worked out from its own shop's rows alone, so a row from Hill never reaches Bay's total.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df.groupby('shop', as_index=False)['units'].sum()

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units  price
0   Bay      2      5
1  Hill      1      8
2   Bay      3      5
3  Hill      4      8

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units  price
0   Bay      2      5
1  Hill      1      8
2   Bay      3      5
3  Hill      4      8

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df.groupby('shop', as_index=False)['units'].mean()

values.name: df
values.display:
shop  units  price
0   Bay      2      5
1  Hill      1      8
2   Bay      3      5
3  Hill      4      8

lead.text: Groups raise a counting question. Suppose Bay has two orders and one of them has no units recorded, while Hill has a single order of 4 units. Bay's group holds two rows but only one known value. pandas has a separate tool for each count.

size counts the rows in a group, whether or not they hold data. count, applied to a column, counts only the entries in that column that are known. In Bay's group size gives 2 and count gives 1. A third tool, nunique, counts the different values in a column and counts a repeated value once, so for the entries 'red', 'blue', 'red' and 'red' it gives 2.

Which count you want depends on the question. How many orders came in is a question for size. How many orders have a usable number of units is a question for count. Mixing the two up is a quiet way to misreport a group.
size counts every row in a group. count on a column counts only the entries that are known.

reveal.text: Missing entries are still rows, so size counts them. count leaves them out because they are not known values.

steps.headline: When the key itself is missing

lead.text: The shop name that groups the rows can be missing too. By default groupby drops any row whose key is missing, as if it were not there. Those rows then vanish from the report, and its totals come out short without any message.

Passing dropna=False to groupby keeps those rows together as a group of their own. The figure has two cases. The first is the table from the last screen, counting rows and known values for each shop. The second has an order whose shop is missing, summed with dropna=False.

afterFigure.text: In the first case Bay has 2 rows and 1 known value, and Hill has 1 of each. In the second the units add up to 2 for Bay, 4 for Hill and 3 for the group with no shop, so every order is accounted for. Whether to keep that group, repair the key or leave it out is your decision, and the default makes it for you without saying so.

result = df.groupby('shop').agg(rows=('units', 'size'), known=('units', 'count'))

2  Hill    4.0

lead.text: Rows whose group key is missing are dropped by default. groupby(..., dropna=False) keeps them together as a group of their own.

reveal.text: The missing key became a group of its own instead of vanishing. Dropping them silently would have lost those rows from the report.

blocks.text: Four people in a small firm earn 2, 3, 4 and 19 thousand pounds a year. The owner wants one figure to put in a report, and divides the whole wage bill of 28 thousand equally among the four. That gives 7 thousand each. Three of the four earn less than that, and the fourth earns nearly three times as much. Whether 7 is a fair picture of the firm depends on what the figure is meant to say.

Once text and dates are readable, a table needs summarising in just this way. The first choice is which single figure should stand for many values. A table of orders from several shops raises the same choice once per shop, so the work moves inside groups of rows. A column with gaps adds a second problem, since a count of rows and a count of known values stop being the same number.
This lesson starts with the firm's four wages. It then moves on to summaries for each group of rows and ends with counting what is really there.

intro.promise: By the end you'll pick the right summary for a column and work it out for each group.

recap.keyIdea: The mean shares a total and the median finds the middle; groupby summarises inside each group, and count and size answer different questions.

blocks.text: You found that the firm's mean pay is 7 thousand and its median is 3.5. Bay's units total 8 in a grouped sum, and keeping the missing key made 3 groups.

recap.nextHook: Grouped summaries come from one table, but a real report draws on several: orders in one place and customer addresses in another. Bringing them together can change how many rows there are, and a total taken afterwards changes with it. The next lesson stacks and matches tables, and counts the rows before anything is added up.

lessons.title: Combine data without multiplying the answer

lead.text: There are two basic ways to combine tables. The first is stacking, which puts one table under another when both describe the same kind of thing. Two months of orders, kept in separate tables with the same columns, become one list of orders. pd.concat([a, b]) does this and lines the columns up by name.

concat keeps every row of both tables, repeated ones included, so the result has as many rows as the two tables together. It also keeps each row's original index label. If both tables were numbered from 0, the labels repeat, and ignore_index=True renumbers the rows from 0 instead. The figure stacks two small tables of units both ways.

afterFigure.text: Each table has two rows and the stack has four. In the first case the labels read 0, 1, 0, 1, because each table brought its own numbering. In the second they read 0, 1, 2, 3. The value 4 sits in both tables and appears twice in the result, since stacking never checks for repeats. Removing repeats is a separate step that you have to ask for.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 4]})
b = pd.DataFrame({'units': [4, 6]})
result = pd.concat([a, b])

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 4]})
b = pd.DataFrame({'units': [4, 6]})
result = pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)

lead.text: concat keeps every row of both tables. Think about whether anything in the call removes repeats.

reveal.text: You added the row counts. concat stacks the tables and never removes repeated rows.

lead.text: The second way to combine tables is matching. Orders hold a customer number but no address, and the address book holds each number with an address. merge lines the two tables up on a shared column, called the key, so that each order row picks up the address of the customer with the same number. The table whose rows you want to keep is the left one, and here the address book is the right one.

What happens to a row with no partner is a choice. An inner merge keeps only the rows whose key appears in both tables. A left merge keeps every left row and fills the right-hand columns with missing values where nothing matched. The figure merges four orders with a small address book that lacks customer 3, first as an inner merge and then as a left merge. The indicator=True in the second call adds a column that says where each row came from, and validate is explained a little later.

afterFigure.text: Customer 3 has an order but no address. The inner merge drops that order, so it returns 3 rows. The left merge keeps the order with a missing region, so it returns all 4. Neither choice is wrong, because they answer different questions. The inner merge gives the orders that can be described. The left merge gives every order and shows which have no address. For a sales report the left merge is usually safer, since it cannot lose an order without saying so.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'customer': [1, 1, 2, 3], 'amount': [10, 20, 15, 8]})
people = pd.DataFrame({'customer': [1, 2, 4], 'region': ['East', 'West', 'East']})
result = orders.merge(people, on='customer', how='inner', validate='many_to_one')

1         1      20   East
2         2      15   West

people = pd.DataFrame({'customer': [1, 2, 4], 'region': ['East', 'West', 'East']})

steps.headline: Left keys are 4, 4, 4, 5 and 6. Unique right keys are 4 and 5. How many rows do an inner merge and a left merge return?

workedSteps.text: Inner: each left 4 matches the right 4, and the left 5 matches the right 5. The 6 has no match.
Left: the same four matches, plus the unmatched 6 with missing right-side values.

steps.headline: The left table has keys 1 through 3. The right table has keys 1 and 2, each once. How many rows does a left merge return?

workedSteps.text: Which left keys have a match on the right? How many?
A left merge also keeps the unmatched left row. How many rows does it return in all?

lead.text: Matching assumes each key picks out one row on the right. That holds for an address book that lists every customer once, so an order picks up a single address and the number of rows stays the same. If the right-hand table repeats a key, every left row with that key is matched with every right row that has it.

That is how the double-listed customer causes trouble. Four orders, each matched with two copies of the address, become eight lines. Nothing fails and no warning appears, and a total taken afterwards counts each order twice. The check is validate='many_to_one', which allows many left rows to share a key but requires each right key to appear once. If the right table breaks the rule, merge raises an error and stops. The figure shows the check passing on a tidy lookup table, and then a merge with no check on a table that repeats a key.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the lookup lists id 1 once, so the two left rows each find one partner and the result has 2 rows. In the second, id 1 appears twice on the right, so each of the two left rows pairs with both and the result has 4. The number of matched rows for a key is its count on the left times its count on the right. A merge that returns more rows than the left table held is the signal to look for repeated keys.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 1], 'amount': [5, 7]})
b = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1], 'region': ['East']})
result = a.merge(b, on='id', validate='many_to_one')

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 1], 'amount': [5, 7]})
b = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 1], 'region': ['East', 'West']})
result = a.merge(b, on='id')

1   1       5   West
2   1       7   East
3   1       7   West

lead.text: The right-hand table is the lookup, and a repeated key there is what multiplies rows. Pick the setting that guards against it.
Every left row with a key pairs with every right row that has the same key.

reveal.text: Each of the left rows paired with each right row, so the counts multiplied. Totals taken after such a join count amounts several times.

lead.text: One more trap sits in the key columns. A missing key is unknown, so you might expect two of them never to match. In a pandas merge, two missing keys do match each other. A row with no id then picks up whatever the right table holds under its own missing id, and the result looks complete.
The figure merges tables whose ids are 1 and a missing value. The first case merges them as they are. The second drops the rows with a missing id from the right-hand table first.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the second left row, whose id is missing, picks up the region 'Unknown' from the right row that also has a missing id. That order has no known customer, so it should have no region. In the second case the missing id is dropped from the right-hand table before the merge, so nothing matches it and the region stays missing. Before you trust a merge, count the missing values in both key columns and decide what should happen to them.

lead.text: Two missing keys can match each other in a pandas merge. Think about what each left row finds on the right.

reveal.text: The two missing keys matched, so a row picked up data it should not have. Decide whether missing keys should match, be rejected or stay unmatched.

blocks.text: A customer has placed four orders. By mistake, the address book lists that customer twice, with the same address on both lines. A report is meant to attach an address to every order, so it matches each order against the address book. Nobody expects the customer to show up as anything other than four lines.

Summaries come from one table, but a real report draws on several. Two tables can be stacked one under the other, or matched row by row through a shared column such as a customer number. Either way the number of rows can change, and every total taken afterwards changes with it. The danger is a report that is wrong while every figure in it looks reasonable.
This lesson follows the double-listed customer through stacking and matching. It counts the rows at each step, because the count is the cheapest check there is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll stack tables, match them by key, and predict how many rows a join returns before you total anything.

recap.keyIdea: concat stacks rows without deduplicating, merge matches by key, and repeated keys multiply rows, so count the rows a join returns before totalling.

blocks.text: You found that the double-listed customer shows 8 order lines. A left merge kept 3 rows for keys 1 to 3, and matching missing keys gave 2 rows a region.

recap.nextHook: Matching leaves a table with the right rows, but the layout may still suit the computer better than the reader. A report often wants shops down the side and months across the top, while the data arrives as a long list with one row for each shop and month. The next lesson turns a list into a grid and back again without changing what any figure means.

lessons.title: Change the layout without losing the meaning

steps.headline: From a list to a grid

lead.text: The list has one row per record, and the grid has one cell per record. df.pivot(index='shop', columns='month', values='units') builds the grid. The shop values become the row labels, the month values become the column headings, and each units figure moves into the cell where its shop row meets its month column. Nothing is added or changed on the way, so a pivot only rearranges the records.

A cell holds one value, so pivot needs each shop and month pair to appear once. It also matters which way round you ask. The figure pivots four records twice, once with the shops down the side and once with the months.

afterFigure.text: Both grids hold the same four figures. Bay has 2 under Jan and 5 under Feb, and Hill has 3 under Jan and 7 under Feb. In the second grid the figures are the same and the months run down the side. Swapping index and columns turns one into the other. If a pair appeared twice, pivot could not choose between the two figures and would stop with an error, which is what the next screen deals with.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 5, 3, 7]})
result = df.pivot(index='shop', columns='month', values='units')

shop           
Bay      5    2
Hill     7    3

result = df.pivot(index='month', columns='shop', values='units')
